moments.title: Miescher isolates 'nuclein'
moments.body:
A 25-year-old Swiss chemist works on pus-stained bandages collected from a nearby hospital. From the white blood cells he isolates a strange phosphorus-rich substance from the nucleus. He calls it nuclein.

No one knows what it does. Most biochemists assume proteins carry hereditary information — nuclein looks too simple to do that job.

quote.text: It seems probable that nuclein represents a whole group of slightly different substances.

moments.takeaway: We had the molecule for 75 years before we knew it was the hereditary material.

moments.title: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty
moments.who: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty, Rockefeller Institute
moments.body:
Building on Griffith's 1928 transformation experiment, they show that the substance which converts harmless pneumococcus into virulent ones is DNA, not protein. They digest the active extract with various enzymes; only DNase destroys activity.

The paper is met with skepticism. Many biochemists are convinced proteins must be the hereditary material — DNA has only four bases, surely too few to encode life's diversity.
moments.takeaway: DNA is the hereditary material — but no one knows what it looks like or how it copies.

moments.title: Hershey-Chase blender experiment
moments.who: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase, Cold Spring Harbor
moments.body:
They use bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) with radioactively labelled protein (S-35) or DNA (P-32). When the phages infect bacteria, only the DNA label enters the cells; the protein coat stays outside.

DNA, not protein, carries the genetic information into the bacteria. The remaining holdouts begin accepting the Avery result.
moments.takeaway: Independent confirmation seals the question: DNA carries inheritance.

moments.title: The double helix
moments.who: Watson, Crick — with Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51
moments.body:
Watson (American, 25) and Crick (British, 36) at the Cavendish Lab build models attempting to fit X-ray diffraction data. The critical evidence — Rosalind Franklin's beautiful Photo 51, taken at King's College London — is shown to them WITHOUT HER PERMISSION by Maurice Wilkins.

Watson and Crick propose the double helix in a one-page paper in Nature: two antiparallel strands held together by A-T and G-C base pairs.

quote.text: It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.

moments.takeaway: Structure suggests function — base pairing IS the copying mechanism.

moments.title: Meselson-Stahl confirms semiconservative replication
moments.who: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl, Caltech
moments.body:
Bacteria are grown in N-15 medium (heavy nitrogen), then switched to N-14. After one round of replication, all DNA is intermediate-density (one heavy strand, one light). After two rounds, half is intermediate and half is fully light.

The result is exactly what Watson and Crick predicted: each parental strand serves as a template for a new daughter strand.

Meselson and Stahl's work has been called 'the most beautiful experiment in biology'.
moments.takeaway: DNA replicates semiconservatively. The base-pairing copying mechanism is real.

now.title: DNA today
now.body:
The human genome contains ~3 billion base pairs across 23 chromosome pairs. We've sequenced thousands of species. CRISPR-Cas9 lets us edit any DNA sequence. Single-molecule sequencing reads entire chromosomes end-to-end.

DNA-based data storage (Microsoft and others) writes information into synthetic DNA at densities exceeding 200 PB per gram. We engineer organisms (synthetic biology) by writing in custom DNA sequences.
now.open_questions: Why does so much DNA appear functionless? What's the role of three-dimensional folding (topologically associated domains) in gene regulation? Can we use synthetic biology to design genomes from scratch? Why do some mutations cause disease while genetically identical mutations in different people don't?

items.reflection: Rosalind Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 — four years before the Nobel Prize that went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins. Watson's autobiography 'The Double Helix' described her in patronising terms. He later expressed regret. How should the history of science treat the contributions of people who weren't given credit at the time?

moments.title: Voyage of the Beagle
moments.body:
A 22-year-old Charles Darwin signs on as gentleman naturalist aboard HMS Beagle. The voyage lasts almost five years. He collects fossils in Patagonia, observes glaciation in Tierra del Fuego, and visits the Galapagos in September 1835.

The Galapagos finches and mockingbirds especially catch his attention. He notes that each island has its own subtly different species — though he doesn't realise the full significance at the time.
moments.takeaway: Five years of natural-history observation, organised by Lyell's recently-published Principles of Geology, set up everything that follows.

moments.title: Darwin reads Malthus
moments.body:
Darwin reads Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population. Malthus had argued that human populations grow geometrically while food supplies grow arithmetically, leading to inevitable competition and culling.

Darwin realises the same logic applies to ALL species — and that variations giving any reproductive advantage would be amplified by repeated culling. The mechanism of natural selection clicks into place.

quote.text: I happened to read for amusement Malthus on Population, and being well prepared to appreciate the struggle for existence... it at once struck me that under these circumstances favourable variations would tend to be preserved.

moments.takeaway: Darwin has the mechanism. He doesn't publish for 20 years.

moments.title: Wallace's letter
moments.who: Alfred Russel Wallace (in Indonesia) and Darwin (in England)
moments.body:
Wallace, a self-funded naturalist working in the Malay Archipelago, writes Darwin a letter laying out essentially the same theory of natural selection. The shock spurs Darwin into action.

Lyell and Hooker arrange for a joint presentation of Darwin's earlier (unpublished) notes and Wallace's paper at the Linnaean Society in July 1858. Almost no one notices. The Society's president remarks that the year produced 'no striking discoveries'.
moments.takeaway: Two naturalists arrive independently at the same idea. Darwin is forced to publish.

moments.title: On the Origin of Species
moments.body:
Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection. The first 1,250-copy print run sells out on the day of publication. It is a careful, evidence-rich book — Darwin understood the controversy he was unleashing.

He does not mention humans in the book, except in one famously brief sentence: 'Light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.'

quote.text: There is grandeur in this view of life... from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.

moments.takeaway: The biological foundation of modern biology is published. Controversy is immediate.

moments.title: Modern synthesis
moments.who: Theodosius Dobzhansky, Ernst Mayr, Julian Huxley, others
moments.body:
Darwin had no mechanism of inheritance. Mendelian genetics (rediscovered around 1900) at first appeared inconsistent with selection. The 'modern synthesis' of the 1930s and 40s shows population genetics, Mendelian inheritance and Darwinian selection are all one consistent theory.

Dobzhansky's 1937 'Genetics and the Origin of Species' is the classic synthesis text.
moments.takeaway: Darwin's selection plus Mendel's genetics give modern evolutionary biology its mathematical foundation.

now.title: Evolution today
now.body:
Evolution underlies all biology. Genome sequencing tracks evolutionary change in real time (antibiotic resistance, viral mutation, agricultural pests). We reconstruct phylogenies, observe speciation events, and trace human ancestry back through 6 million years and ancient DNA back to 1.6 million years ago.

Mechanisms beyond selection: genetic drift, gene flow, neutral evolution, horizontal gene transfer, hybridisation, sexual selection, kin selection.
now.open_questions: What's the role of major transitions (origin of life, cells, multicellularity) — chance or law? How predictable is evolution? (E. coli experiments: more than people thought.) What's the relative contribution of selection vs drift in genome evolution? Can evolutionary principles be applied to other complex systems (memes, languages, software)?

items.reflection: Wallace had the same idea as Darwin and never received equal credit. He always referred to the theory as 'Darwinism' himself. He also became a spiritualist later in life, which embarrassed Darwin's circle. How does science treat the 'second discoverer' — and the discoverer who later holds unscientific beliefs?

moments.title: Mendel's pea experiments
moments.who: Gregor Mendel, monastery garden at Brünn (Brno)
moments.body:
Mendel, an Augustinian friar with training in physics and statistics, raises tens of thousands of pea plants and tracks seven discrete characteristics: seed shape, seed colour, pod shape, etc.

He crosses plants with contrasting traits. He sees that one trait disappears in F1 hybrids, reappears in F2 at exactly 3:1 ratios. He correctly infers there are pairs of discrete 'factors' (later called alleles), one from each parent, with dominant and recessive variants.
moments.takeaway: Inheritance is particulate, not blending. Discrete factors with predictable ratios.

moments.title: Mendel publishes
moments.who: Gregor Mendel, Proceedings of the Brünn Natural History Society
moments.body:
Mendel reads his results at two meetings and publishes them as 'Experiments on Plant Hybrids' in the local society proceedings. The journal goes to 120 libraries across Europe.

The paper is read by perhaps a few dozen people. It is cited only three times in the next 35 years. Mendel sends a copy to Carl von Nägeli, a leading botanist, who suggests he repeat his work with hawkweeds — which (unbeknownst to either) reproduce asexually most of the time. Mendel's results don't replicate. He gradually gives up biological research and rises in the monastic hierarchy.
moments.takeaway: The foundational paper of genetics is ignored for 34 years. A single piece of advice steers Mendel away from confirming his own theory.

moments.title: Rediscovery
moments.who: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak — independently
moments.body:
Three botanists, working independently, rediscover Mendel's laws within months of each other. Each searches the older literature for precedents and finds Mendel's 1866 paper. All three credit him generously in their first papers.

Mendel is suddenly famous, 16 years after his death.
moments.takeaway: The same discovery comes to three different people, all of whom find Mendel had it first. Science sometimes rewards the dead.

moments.title: Morgan's flies link genes to chromosomes
moments.body:
Morgan and his students breed thousands of fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) in a Columbia office that becomes famous as 'the fly room'. They map mutations to specific positions on specific chromosomes.

Morgan's lab demonstrates that 'genes' are real physical entities on chromosomes, with measurable recombination distances. The chromosome theory of inheritance is established.
moments.takeaway: Genes have material reality. They are arranged linearly on chromosomes, with calculable distances between them.

now.title: Genetics today
now.body:
We've moved from Mendel's discrete factors to genome-wide association studies (GWAS), polygenic scores, and direct sequencing of single cells. We routinely identify the gene responsible for a Mendelian disorder within months of recognising it. Population-scale genomics maps human history.

CRISPR-Cas9 lets us edit specific genes in living organisms. Gene therapy is starting to work for previously untreatable conditions (sickle cell disease, certain blindnesses, spinal muscular atrophy).
now.open_questions: Most traits are polygenic and complex. How do hundreds of small-effect genes combine? Why do identical twins sometimes differ markedly in phenotype? What are the ethical limits of genome editing — particularly in human embryos? Are there 'IQ genes' and how heavily do environment vs genetics contribute to complex behaviours?

items.reflection: Mendel's pea data are statistically too good — the ratios match expectations almost perfectly. Ronald Fisher noted in 1936 that the probability of such clean data is small. Either Mendel was extraordinarily lucky, or he (or an assistant) selected which crosses to count. Should we hold the founders of disciplines to modern standards of statistical honesty?

moments.title: Semmelweis cuts maternal mortality with handwashing
moments.body:
Semmelweis notices that the maternity ward staffed by doctors (who also dissected cadavers in the morning) has 10 percent maternal mortality from puerperal fever. The ward staffed by midwives has 4 percent. He requires doctors to wash hands in chlorinated lime water between cadaver work and deliveries. Mortality drops to under 1 percent.

He cannot explain WHY. The miasma theory (disease from bad air) and humoral medicine reject his findings. He's dismissed, hospitalised in 1865 in an asylum, beaten by guards and dies of sepsis. Aged 47.
moments.takeaway: Empirical evidence works. Without a theory, it can also be ignored — and the bearer can be persecuted.

moments.title: Snow maps cholera in Soho
moments.body:
London's Broad Street has a cholera outbreak. Dominant theory: cholera spreads via 'miasma' (bad air). Snow, a physician, plots cholera deaths on a street map. They cluster around one water pump. He persuades authorities to remove the pump handle.

Snow doesn't know about the microbe (Vibrio cholerae is identified later by Pacini in 1854, then Koch in 1884). He has the epidemiological evidence that something in the water is responsible.
moments.takeaway: Epidemiology can identify transmission routes before microbiology identifies the agent.

moments.title: Pasteur disproves spontaneous generation
moments.body:
Pasteur designs swan-neck flasks: bent glass tubes that admit air but trap dust and microbes. Sterilised broth in such a flask stays clear indefinitely. Snap the neck off, and the broth grows microbes within hours.

If microbes appeared spontaneously, they should grow in both. They don't. Microbes come from microbes — they don't generate from nothing.

quote.text: Never will the doctrine of spontaneous generation recover from the mortal blow of this simple experiment.

moments.takeaway: Microbial life comes from prior microbial life. Spontaneous generation is dead.

moments.title: Koch's postulates
moments.body:
Koch isolates Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) in 1876 and shows it causes anthrax in mice. In 1882 he isolates Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He formulates the postulates that establish whether a specific microbe causes a specific disease:

1. The microbe must be found in all cases of the disease.
2. It must be isolable in pure culture.
3. Reintroduction into a healthy host must cause the disease.
4. The microbe must be recoverable from the new host.
moments.takeaway: Causality between specific microbes and specific diseases can now be established rigorously.

moments.title: Fleming notices a mould
moments.who: Alexander Fleming, St Mary's Hospital, London
moments.body:
Fleming returns from holiday to find his Petri dishes of Staphylococcus contaminated by a mould. A clear zone of dead bacteria surrounds the mould (Penicillium). He extracts the active substance but cannot purify enough for use.

Florey and Chain at Oxford develop production methods in 1940 and demonstrate penicillin's lifesaving effect. By 1944, the US Army is mass-producing it. Fleming, Florey and Chain share the 1945 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The first antibiotic — found by accident, developed by careful pharmacology. Bacterial infection becomes treatable.

now.title: Infectious disease today
now.body:
Germ theory is the foundation of modern medicine. Childbed fever is rare. Most surgery is safe. Vaccines, antibiotics, antivirals and sterile technique save millions annually.

We sequence pathogens within days of an outbreak. mRNA vaccines were produced against SARS-CoV-2 within months. Antibiotic resistance is a major global threat — bacteria evolve.
now.open_questions: Can we develop new antibiotics fast enough to keep up with resistance? Can we make universal vaccines (influenza, coronaviruses)? What's the next pandemic likely to be? How do we control vector-borne diseases (mosquitoes, ticks) as climate changes their ranges?

items.reflection: Semmelweis was right and died in a mental institution. Snow's discovery of cholera transmission was rejected for decades. Pasteur and Koch faced fierce resistance. Why is medicine particularly resistant to changes in its theoretical foundations, even when the empirical evidence is overwhelming?

moments.title: Fleming's contaminated plate
moments.who: Alexander Fleming, St Mary's Hospital, London
moments.body:
Fleming returns from holiday to find an opened Petri dish of Staphylococcus has been contaminated by a Penicillium mould blown in from a neighbouring mycology lab. Around the mould, a clear zone shows where the staph cells have been killed.

Fleming publishes the observation in 1929 and calls the active substance penicillin. He cannot purify it, doses mice and finds it is not toxic, but cannot make enough to treat anyone.
moments.takeaway: Discovery is partly luck and partly a prepared mind. Fleming had been on the lookout for antibacterial substances since WWI.

moments.title: Florey, Chain and Heatley scale up penicillin
moments.who: Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, Norman Heatley — Oxford
moments.body:
An Oxford team takes up penicillin production. Heatley invents a system of bedpans to grow it in volume. By 1940 they have enough to test in mice: infected with streptococci, treated mice survive, untreated die.

The first human patient (1941): policeman Albert Alexander, with a scratch turned septic, recovers dramatically when given penicillin — until the supply runs out. He relapses and dies. The team realise they cannot make enough.
moments.takeaway: Penicillin works in humans. Production is now the limiting factor.

moments.title: US mass production
moments.body:
The US Department of Agriculture lab in Peoria finds a Penicillium strain (on a mouldy cantaloupe at the local market) that produces 100 times more penicillin than the Oxford strain. Deep tank fermentation lets Pfizer scale to industrial volumes.

By D-Day (June 1944), enough penicillin is available to treat every Allied soldier. Casualties from infected wounds plummet.
moments.takeaway: Industrial-scale antibiotic production transforms warfare and surgery.

moments.title: Fleming's warning
moments.body:
In his Nobel Prize acceptance speech, Fleming warns that overuse of penicillin will inevitably select for resistant bacteria. He notes the ease with which lab strains become resistant.

Less than a decade later, hospital-acquired Staphylococcus aureus is showing widespread resistance. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) emerges by 1961.

quote.text: It is not difficult to make microbes resistant to penicillin in the laboratory... There is the danger that the ignorant man may easily underdose himself, and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug make them resistant.

moments.takeaway: The man who discovered the first antibiotic predicted resistance from the start.

moments.title: Golden age of antibiotic discovery
moments.body:
Streptomycin (Selman Waksman's lab, 1943), chloramphenicol (1947), tetracyclines (1948), erythromycin (1952), vancomycin (1958), methicillin (1959). Every major antibiotic class is discovered between 1940 and 1962.

After 1962, almost no new structural classes are found. Most modern 'new' antibiotics are derivatives of older ones.
moments.takeaway: The antibiotic discovery pipeline shrinks. We are running out of new structural classes.

now.title: Antibiotics today
now.body:
Antibiotic resistance kills an estimated 1.27 million people per year globally (Lancet 2022). Many infections we treated easily 20 years ago are now becoming hard or impossible to cure.

WHO maintains a 'critical priority' list of resistant pathogens. New mechanisms (CRISPR-based antibiotics, bacteriophages, anti-virulence drugs) are being explored.
now.open_questions: Will we find genuinely new antibiotic classes? Can phage therapy scale? Can we make antibiotic stewardship work globally? Is veterinary antibiotic use (much larger than human use) the key driver of resistance? How can pharma fund research on drugs that won't be used much, by design, to delay resistance?

items.reflection: Fleming, Florey, Chain and Heatley all contributed essential pieces. The 1945 Nobel honoured the first three but not Heatley, whose practical engineering was indispensable. Florey often said 'penicillin saved millions because Norman Heatley figured out how to grow it.' How does scientific recognition value the engineering and craft work that turns a discovery into a treatment?

moments.title: The coding problem
moments.body:
Once DNA's structure was known, the question became: how does a sequence of four nucleotides specify a sequence of 20 amino acids?

George Gamow (physicist) proposes in 1954 that codons of three nucleotides each, in overlapping fashion, would give 64 combinations — enough for 20 amino acids. The 'codon' concept is born.
moments.takeaway: A coding problem in molecular biology, attacked by mathematical reasoning before any biological experiments could test it.

moments.title: Nirenberg and Matthaei crack the first codon
moments.body:
Nirenberg and his postdoc Heinrich Matthaei set up a cell-free system: ribosomes, transfer RNAs, amino acids, and synthetic messenger RNA. They add a synthetic mRNA made entirely of U's (poly-U).

The system makes a polypeptide consisting entirely of phenylalanine. UUU codes for phenylalanine. The first codon is cracked.
moments.takeaway: An entire vocabulary can be decoded one word at a time.

moments.title: Crick, Brenner, Barnett and Watts-Tobin — triplet code
moments.who: Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner and colleagues, Cambridge
moments.body:
Working with bacteriophage T4 mutants, they introduce frameshift mutations (insertions or deletions of nucleotides). The pattern of which combinations restore function shows the genetic code reads in NON-OVERLAPPING triplets.

The paper is published months after Nirenberg's poly-U result. Together they establish: the code is triplet, non-overlapping, has no spacers.
moments.takeaway: Genetic information is read in non-overlapping triplets. The grammar of the code is clear.

moments.title: Filling in the codon table
moments.who: Marshall Nirenberg, Severo Ochoa, Har Gobind Khorana — and others
moments.body:
A race to decode every codon. Nirenberg's lab uses synthetic mRNAs of mixed composition. Ochoa's lab uses random copolymers. Khorana's lab synthesises mRNAs with known repeating patterns (UCUCUC..., UCAUCAUCA...).

By 1966 all 64 codons are assigned. 61 code for amino acids; 3 are stop codons. AUG is the start codon, encoding methionine. The code is degenerate (multiple codons per amino acid) but unambiguous (no codon codes for two amino acids).
moments.takeaway: The genetic code is universal (almost). Bacteria, plants, animals — same codons, same amino acids.

moments.title: Nobel Prize and the central dogma confirmed
moments.body:
Nirenberg and Khorana share the 1968 Nobel Prize with Robert Holley, who had determined the first complete sequence of a transfer RNA (alanine tRNA from yeast) in 1965.

The central dogma — DNA → RNA → protein — now has all the components mapped. The vocabulary, syntax and machinery are known.
moments.takeaway: Molecular biology has its first complete operating manual.

now.title: The genetic code today
now.body:
The code is now known in extraordinary detail. Mitochondria use a slightly different code in some organisms. Some unicellular eukaryotes reassign stop codons.

We can read the entire genome of any organism. We can synthesise long DNA sequences (megabase scale). We can rewrite codons (genome recoding) to engineer organisms with expanded genetic codes — adding novel amino acids not found in nature.
now.open_questions: Why is the code (largely) universal? Is it frozen accident, or optimal in some sense? Why are some codon assignments asymmetric (Trp uses one codon, Leu uses six)? Can we design organisms with fundamentally different genetic systems? What was the genetic code of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?

items.reflection: Nirenberg was working at the NIH on what many considered an obscure problem. He was bypassed by the famous molecular biologists (Watson, Crick, Brenner) who had assumed cracking the code would require their kind of clever phage genetics. Nirenberg's brute-force biochemistry won the race. Sometimes ingenuity beats brilliance — does prestige bias predict who gets the breakthrough wrong as often as it predicts it right?

moments.title: Proposing to sequence the human genome
moments.who: Robert Sinsheimer, Renato Dulbecco, James Watson, others
moments.body:
By the mid-1980s, sequencing was possible but slow (hundreds of bases per day per machine). Some biologists, including Sinsheimer, proposed a coordinated effort to sequence the entire human genome.

Opposition was fierce. Most molecular biologists thought it was a waste of money and resources. James Watson became the first director of the National Center for Human Genome Research in 1990 (resigning in 1992 over disagreements about gene patents).
moments.takeaway: Big-science genome sequencing began as a contested idea. The community was split.

moments.title: First full genome — Haemophilus influenzae
moments.who: Craig Venter and Hamilton Smith, TIGR
moments.body:
Venter's team uses shotgun sequencing (random fragments, computational assembly) to sequence Haemophilus influenzae — 1.8 million bases. The first complete genome of any free-living organism.

Within a year, more bacterial genomes and the first archaeon (Methanocaldococcus jannaschii) follow. Comparative genomics is born.
moments.takeaway: Whole-genome sequencing is now possible. The bacterial 'tree of life' becomes mappable in detail.

moments.title: The race
moments.who: International Human Genome Project vs Celera Genomics (Venter)
moments.body:
The international Human Genome Project, led by Francis Collins, had planned a slow, careful clone-by-clone sequencing. In 1998, Venter founded Celera Genomics with a plan to sequence the human genome faster (and patent gene sequences).

The race ran for 2 years. The NIH and Wellcome Trust public consortium accelerated dramatically in response. Both groups announced draft genomes at the White House on 26 June 2000, with Tony Blair joining remotely. Both papers appeared in Nature and Science in February 2001.
moments.takeaway: Public and private efforts produced a draft of the human genome in parallel. Competition (and the threat of patents) accelerated the work.

moments.title: Complete (mostly) sequence
moments.body:
On 14 April 2003 — the 50th anniversary of Watson and Crick's double helix paper — the HGP announces a 'complete' human genome: 92 percent of the euchromatin, with very high accuracy. The remaining 8 percent (heterochromatic, repetitive regions) defeats the technology of the time.

The project took 13 years and cost about $3 billion in total. It comes in under budget and ahead of schedule.
moments.takeaway: Most of the human genome is now in databases. Personalised medicine and genome-wide association studies become possible.

moments.title: Telomere-to-telomere genome
moments.body:
The Telomere-to-Telomere consortium, using long-read sequencing technologies (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore), publishes the first truly complete human genome — including the formerly intractable centromeres, telomeres and ribosomal DNA repeats. About 8 percent of the genome had been missing.

The 'reference genome' becomes a pangenome: hundreds of individuals from diverse populations capture more of human genetic variation.
moments.takeaway: It took 19 more years to finish the last 8 percent. The most complex regions of the genome required completely new sequencing technologies.

now.title: Genomes today
now.body:
Sequencing costs have dropped from $3 billion (HGP, 13 years) to under $200 (a few days). The 100,000 Genomes Project (UK, completed 2018) and All of Us (US, ongoing, target 1 million) collect genomes for biomedical research.

Genome editing (CRISPR-Cas9) lets us modify any sequence. Gene therapies for sickle cell disease, hereditary blindness and spinal muscular atrophy have been approved.
now.open_questions: How much of common disease risk can be predicted from polygenic scores? How do non-coding variants affect gene regulation? Can we use synthetic biology to design genomes from scratch? What are the ethical and equity implications of widespread genetic testing? How do we prevent genetic information misuse?

items.reflection: Venter was widely accused of trying to privatise human genetic information. Celera withdrew its patent claims under pressure. The public HGP made all data immediately public (the Bermuda Principles, 1996). Without that policy, modern genomics might look very different. How do we balance commercial incentives against open science when the stakes are this high?

moments.title: Strange repeats in E. coli
moments.body:
Ishino's group is studying an unrelated bacterial gene. They notice odd clusters of short, repeating DNA sequences separated by 'spacer' sequences in the bacterium's genome. They report the observation but do not know what it is.

Similar repeats are found in many other bacteria over the next decade. They are named CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) by Francisco Mojica in 2002.
moments.takeaway: A peculiar genomic feature is catalogued for 20 years before anyone understands its function.

moments.title: Mojica's hypothesis
moments.body:
Mojica realises that the 'spacers' between CRISPR repeats match sequences from bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria). He hypothesises CRISPR is a bacterial immune system: bacteria capture pieces of phage DNA and store them as 'memories' to recognise the phage on future encounters.

His paper is rejected by several journals before publication.
moments.takeaway: Bacteria have an adaptive immune system. Almost no one notices.

moments.title: Barrangou and Horvath confirm CRISPR immunity
moments.who: Rodolphe Barrangou and Philippe Horvath, Danisco
moments.body:
Working at the yogurt company Danisco, Barrangou and Horvath show that adding phage DNA sequences to CRISPR spacers makes bacteria resistant to that phage. CRISPR is indeed an adaptive immune system.

Danisco starts using engineered Streptococcus thermophilus to make yogurt cultures resistant to phage contamination.
moments.takeaway: An entire bacterial adaptive immune system was first commercialised by a yogurt company.

moments.title: Doudna and Charpentier programmable cutting
moments.body:
Doudna and Charpentier show that Cas9 — a protein in the CRISPR system — can be programmed with a simple guide RNA to cut any DNA sequence the experimenter chooses. They publish in Science.

The paper is one of the most cited in biology this century. CRISPR-Cas9 becomes a universal genome-editing tool.

quote.text: We show that Cas9 can be programmed by a single chimeric RNA to introduce site-specific double-strand breaks in DNA.
quote.attrib: Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna, Charpentier — Science 2012

moments.takeaway: A bacterial immune system becomes the most powerful gene-editing tool ever developed.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body:
Doudna and Charpentier share the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing. A patent dispute between Berkeley (Doudna) and the Broad Institute (Feng Zhang) over who first developed CRISPR for use in mammalian cells continues for years.

In 2018, Chinese scientist He Jiankui used CRISPR to edit the embryos of twin girls (claiming HIV resistance). He was sentenced to three years in prison. The international community broadly condemned the work as unethical and premature.
moments.takeaway: A Nobel Prize, an ongoing patent war, and the first germline-edited humans — all within eight years of the 2012 paper.

now.title: CRISPR today
now.body:
CRISPR-Cas9 has been used in thousands of laboratories worldwide. New variants (Cas12, Cas13, base editors, prime editors) extend its capabilities. The first CRISPR therapy (Casgevy for sickle cell disease) was approved in 2023.

Applications: agricultural traits, disease research, possible cures for many genetic disorders.
now.open_questions: How do we make off-target editing acceptably rare? Is germline editing ever ethical? Can we deliver CRISPR safely to specific tissues in vivo? Should we use it for human enhancement (not just disease cure)? How do we govern dual-use risks (CRISPR could in principle make pathogens worse)?

items.reflection: Mojica spent years on a research problem that had no obvious applications and that journals rejected. Without his persistence, CRISPR might not have been recognised as an immune system. Basic research often looks pointless until it becomes essential. How should society fund science whose value is unknowable in advance?

moments.title: Hooke sees cells in cork
moments.body:
Hooke, working with a primitive microscope, looks at a slice of cork. He sees small empty chambers — 'cells', he says, because they remind him of monks' rooms. He publishes the observation in Micrographia (1665), one of the first illustrated scientific books.

The cells he sees are dead — just the walls of plant cells. He doesn't see the contents, doesn't understand the structure, and doesn't generalise to other organisms.
moments.takeaway: The word 'cell' enters biology. The biological significance takes nearly two centuries to emerge.

moments.title: Van Leeuwenhoek's 'animalcules'
moments.body:
A self-taught microscope maker, van Leeuwenhoek produces single-lens microscopes magnifying up to 270x — far better than Hooke's. He sees moving creatures in pond water, dental plaque, vinegar. He calls them 'animalcules'.

The Royal Society in London is skeptical until they send observers. Van Leeuwenhoek is the first person to see bacteria.
moments.takeaway: A whole microbial world is visible — but no one knows what to make of it for another two centuries.

moments.title: Schleiden and Schwann formalise cell theory
moments.who: Matthias Schleiden (botanist) and Theodor Schwann (zoologist), Berlin
moments.body:
Schleiden proposes that all plant tissues are composed of cells (1838). Schwann generalises to animals (1839), proposing that all living organisms are made of cells.

They are right but their mechanism (free-cell formation, like crystallisation) is wrong. Cells, they thought, formed by aggregation of formless material.
moments.takeaway: All life is cellular. The unifying principle of modern biology is in place.

moments.title: Virchow — omnis cellula e cellula
moments.body:
Virchow corrects Schleiden and Schwann: cells do not form spontaneously, they come from pre-existing cells. 'Omnis cellula e cellula' — every cell from a cell.

This closes the loop: cells are the units of life, and they reproduce. Combined with germ theory, this overturns spontaneous generation at every scale.

quote.text: Where a cell exists, there must have been a preexisting cell.

moments.takeaway: Cells come from cells. Biology has its first universal generalisation about how life perpetuates.

now.title: Cells today
now.body:
Cell biology is a discipline of its own. Fluorescence microscopy (Nobel 2014 for super-resolution: Betzig, Hell, Moerner) lets us see structures at 20-nanometre resolution. Live-cell imaging tracks single molecules. Single-cell sequencing reveals heterogeneity within tissues.

We understand cells as integrated systems: organelles, cytoskeleton, signaling networks. Synthetic biology engineers cells for purpose-built functions.
now.open_questions: How did the first cell originate? What's the minimal set of genes for a free-living cell (Venter's lab made one with 473 genes in 2016)? Can we build a cell from scratch (bottom-up)? Why do some unicellular organisms become multicellular?

items.reflection: Hooke's word 'cell' was a casual descriptive choice — based on how the cork looked. Two centuries later it had become the most fundamental concept in biology. How much does scientific language shape the development of theory, and how much does theory force a re-evaluation of language?

moments.title: Jenner inoculates James Phipps
moments.body:
Jenner, a country doctor, notices that milkmaids who had had cowpox seemed never to catch smallpox. He takes pus from a milkmaid's cowpox lesion, scratches the arm of an 8-year-old boy named James Phipps, and lets the inoculation site develop. Phipps gets mild cowpox. Six weeks later, Jenner deliberately exposes Phipps to smallpox.

Phipps doesn't get sick.
moments.takeaway: The first vaccination. Jenner takes the rural folk-wisdom and tests it methodically.

moments.title: Jenner publishes
moments.body:
Jenner publishes 'An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae' — 'vaccinia' being his name for the cowpox material. The Royal Society had rejected an earlier version.

Vaccination (from Latin vacca, cow) spreads across Britain and Europe. By 1840 it is mandatory in many places. By the early 20th century, smallpox death rates have plummeted.
moments.takeaway: Smallpox vaccine is the first universal vaccination. Public health takes on a new tool.

moments.title: Pasteur extends vaccination
moments.body:
Pasteur shows that attenuated (weakened) cultures of pathogens confer immunity. He produces vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax (1881, demonstrated dramatically at Pouilly-le-Fort), and rabies (1885, first used on a 9-year-old boy named Joseph Meister).

Vaccination becomes generalisable: any pathogen can in principle be weakened or killed and used to induce immunity.
moments.takeaway: Vaccination becomes a general method, not a single trick for smallpox.

moments.title: Salk's polio vaccine
moments.body:
Polio had become a feared childhood disease, paralysing thousands every year. Salk develops a killed-virus vaccine (1955). A massive field trial (1.8 million children) shows it is safe and effective.

Salk refuses to patent the vaccine. Asked who owned the patent, he replied: 'There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Albert Sabin's oral live-attenuated vaccine (1961) replaces it for most uses.
moments.takeaway: Polio is effectively controlled in industrialised countries within a decade.

moments.title: Smallpox declared eradicated
moments.body:
The last natural smallpox case was in Somalia in 1977. After global ring-vaccination campaigns and intense surveillance, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 — the first (and to date only) human disease completely eradicated.

No smallpox exists anywhere in nature. Stocks remain in two designated laboratories (Atlanta and Koltsovo, Russia) for research.
moments.takeaway: A disease that killed hundreds of millions of people is gone from Earth.

now.title: Vaccines today
now.body:
Vaccines exist for over 25 infectious diseases. mRNA vaccine technology (decades in development) was deployed against COVID-19 within a year of the pandemic's start, saving millions of lives. Cancer mRNA vaccines are in clinical trials.

Vaccine hesitancy — declining trust in scientific institutions — has caused outbreaks of formerly controlled diseases like measles.
now.open_questions: Can we eradicate polio? (Almost — but persistence in conflict zones is a barrier.) Will we ever have an HIV vaccine? A universal influenza vaccine? A malaria vaccine? (The first malaria vaccines have been approved 2021-2023 but are only partially effective.) How do we restore public trust in vaccination?

items.reflection: Jenner's first 'patient' was an eight-year-old boy whose consent was given by his parents in exchange for shelter. James Phipps remained Jenner's friend; Jenner later vaccinated Phipps's son. Modern ethics would not allow Jenner's first trial. How should we judge historical medical practice by modern standards, and what would we have lost if Jenner had not acted?

moments.title: Van Helmont's willow
moments.who: Jan Baptist van Helmont, Vilvoorde (Spanish Netherlands)
moments.body:
Van Helmont plants a 5-pound willow sapling in 200 pounds of dried soil. He waters it for 5 years with rainwater only. At the end, the willow weighs 169 pounds. The soil weighs only 2 ounces less.

He concludes that the willow's mass came from water, not soil. He was partly right (water contributes the H in carbohydrate) — but wrong about the carbon, which comes from atmospheric CO2 that he didn't know existed.
moments.takeaway: Mass had to come from somewhere, and most of it wasn't the soil. The first careful quantitative experiment on plant nutrition.

moments.title: Priestley, mice and Ingenhousz
moments.body:
Priestley shows that a mouse in a sealed jar dies from 'spoiled air'. A sprig of mint placed in the same jar restores it. Plants somehow refresh the air.

Jan Ingenhousz refines this in 1779: the restoration only happens IN SUNLIGHT. In darkness, plants spoil the air like the mouse. He has discovered both the light-dependent and dark phases of photosynthesis without knowing the chemistry.

quote.text: Plants, instead of affecting the air in the same manner with animal respiration, reverse the effects of breathing.

moments.takeaway: Plants produce oxygen, but only when illuminated. Animal respiration and plant photosynthesis are chemically linked.

moments.title: Saussure quantifies
moments.body:
De Saussure shows quantitatively that plants take up CO2 and water, and release oxygen. He measures the masses involved. The basic chemical equation of photosynthesis is now established, decades before the molecular mechanism.

His work is largely ignored for half a century — partly because his German contemporary Justus von Liebig promotes the (incorrect) view that plants get their carbon from soil humus.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative chemistry meets plant biology. The book-keeping of photosynthesis is laid down.

moments.title: Ruben and Kamen with oxygen-18
moments.who: Sam Ruben and Martin Kamen, Berkeley
moments.body:
Using newly available heavy oxygen (O-18), they label either water or CO2 in algae cultures. The released O2 carries the label only when WATER is labelled. The oxygen in photosynthesis comes from splitting water, not from CO2.

Ruben dies in a wartime lab accident in 1943, aged 29. Kamen, who co-discovered carbon-14 the year before, lives on to win the Enrico Fermi Award in 1996.
moments.takeaway: Isotope labelling settles the source of photosynthetic O2. Water is split; CO2 is reduced.

moments.title: Calvin's lollipop and the dark reactions
moments.who: Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson, James Bassham — Berkeley
moments.body:
Calvin's team flasks ('lollipops' — flat glass vessels) hold Chlorella algae. They blast the algae with light, then suddenly pulse them with radioactive C-14 CO2 for a few seconds before killing the cells in hot methanol.

Two-dimensional paper chromatography of the labelled compounds tells them what carbon-fixation products formed first. Over years, they map the entire CO2-fixation cycle — now called the Calvin cycle (or Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle).

Calvin wins the 1961 Nobel Prize. Benson and Bassham, who did much of the experimental work, are not included.

quote.text: Photosynthesis is the most important process on this earth. All the food we eat, all the fossil fuels we burn — these are products of photosynthesis past and present.

moments.takeaway: The dark reactions are mapped step by step. Carbon dioxide becomes sugar via the Calvin cycle.

now.title: Photosynthesis today
now.body:
The light reactions and Calvin cycle are mapped at atomic resolution. Photosystem II crystal structures (2001, 2011) show the water-splitting manganese cluster in detail. Rubisco's flaws are well-characterised. C4 and CAM pathways are understood as carbon-concentrating adaptations.

Applied work: engineering more efficient Rubisco, transplanting C4 traits into C3 crops (RIPE project), artificial photosynthesis for solar fuels, microalgae bioreactors for carbon capture.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer plants with higher photosynthetic efficiency? (Current efficiency is ~1% of incoming solar energy.) Can artificial photosynthesis match plants? What was the photosynthetic pathway of the first cyanobacteria? Why hasn't a higher-efficiency Rubisco evolved naturally?

items.reflection: Van Helmont thought plants grew from water. Priestley thought they 'unspoiled' air. Ingenhousz added light. Saussure added CO2. Ruben and Kamen sourced the O2. Calvin tracked the carbon. Each was right about a piece, wrong about the whole. How does science build correct theories from a sequence of partial truths — and how often do we mistake our current 'partial truth' for the final answer?

moments.title: Krebs proposes the citric acid cycle
moments.body:
Krebs, a Jewish refugee from Germany now at Sheffield, works out the cycle of reactions by which acetyl groups are oxidised to CO2. His 1937 paper is initially rejected by Nature as not warranting urgent publication. Eventually published in Enzymologia.

The cycle — eight reactions in mitochondria — is the central hub of metabolism. Carbohydrates, fats and proteins all funnel into it. Krebs is awarded the 1953 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The central catabolic pathway is mapped. All food converges on the same eight-reaction cycle.

moments.title: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis
moments.who: Peter Mitchell, Glynn House laboratory, Cornwall
moments.body:
Peter Mitchell proposes that ATP synthesis is driven by a proton gradient across the mitochondrial inner membrane, not by a chemical intermediate. The idea is heterodox: most biochemists assumed a high-energy chemical 'squiggle bond' must couple electron transport to ATP formation.

Mitchell's hypothesis is ridiculed. He leaves university research and sets up a private lab in his own house (Glynn) funded by an inheritance. He spends 15 years gathering evidence.

By the 1970s, the chemiosmotic theory is overwhelmingly supported. Mitchell wins the 1978 Nobel Prize.

quote.text: I do not think there is any objective truth in science — only working hypotheses.

moments.takeaway: An outsider's heretical idea is ridiculed, then becomes orthodoxy. Energy is stored as a transmembrane proton gradient.

moments.title: Margulis on endosymbiosis
moments.body:
Lynn Margulis publishes 'On the Origin of Mitosing Cells' (1967), arguing that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by ancestral cells. The paper had been rejected by 15 journals before acceptance.

Her claim: eukaryotic cells are evolutionary chimeras of multiple ancestors. Most biologists dismiss the idea. By the 1980s, molecular evidence (mitochondrial DNA, ribosomes) overwhelmingly supports her.
moments.takeaway: Major evolutionary transitions can happen by merger, not just gradual divergence.

moments.title: Mitchell wins, Margulis vindicated
moments.body:
Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory wins the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 17 years after publication. Margulis is elected to the US National Academy of Sciences in 1983 and receives the National Medal of Science in 1999.

Both had been working against scientific consensus. Both were eventually shown to be right.
moments.takeaway: Both heretical ideas about cellular energy — chemiosmosis and endosymbiosis — became textbook orthodoxy within two decades of being ridiculed.

moments.title: ATP synthase structure
moments.who: John Walker, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge
moments.body:
John Walker solves the X-ray crystal structure of ATP synthase F1 head, revealing the rotary motor at atomic resolution. The enzyme is a literal molecular machine — protons flow through, the rotor turns, and ATP is synthesised at three catalytic sites in sequence.

Walker shares the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Paul Boyer (whose 'binding-change' mechanism predicted the rotation) and Jens Skou (Na/K-ATPase).
moments.takeaway: ATP synthase is the world's smallest rotary motor — and runs in every mitochondrion and chloroplast in every eukaryotic cell.

now.title: Bioenergetics today
now.body:
The full architecture of mitochondrial respiration is known: electron transport chain complexes I-IV, their crystal structures, the proton pumping per complex, ATP synthase rotation. We can image working mitochondria in live cells with fluorescent reporters.

Mitochondrial diseases (~1 in 5000 births) are a recognised category. Mitochondrial replacement therapy ('three-parent babies' approved in UK 2015) prevents transmission. Aging research has implicated mitochondrial decline in cellular senescence.
now.open_questions: Are mitochondrial defects causal in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, ALS? Can we target mitochondria therapeutically? What's the upper limit on ATP synthase rotation rate? How did proton-pumping respiratory chains evolve in the first place? What was the metabolism of LUCA (Last Universal Common Ancestor)?

items.reflection: Mitchell built his own lab when establishment biochemistry rejected his ideas. Margulis submitted to 15 journals before publication. Both eventually shifted the consensus. How does science decide what counts as 'too speculative to consider' — and how do we prevent rejecting future Mitchell-Margulis-class insights when we hear them?

moments.title: Haeckel coins 'ecology'
moments.body:
Ernst Haeckel — a German zoologist, Darwin advocate, and embryologist — coins the term 'Oecologie' for the study of organisms' relations to their environment. 'Oikos' (household) plus 'logia' (study of) — the study of the natural household.

The word takes decades to catch on. Most 19th-century natural history is still done in the older tradition of cataloguing species.
moments.takeaway: Ecology gets its name. The field that will eventually unify biology with environmental science is born.

moments.title: Tansley coins 'ecosystem'
moments.body:
Arthur Tansley publishes 'The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts and Terms' (Ecology, 1935), coining the term 'ecosystem' for the integrated community of organisms together with their physical environment.

He is explicitly reacting against Clements's view of communities as 'superorganisms'. Tansley's ecosystem is a system of energy and matter flows, not a unified being.

quote.text: The whole system, in the sense of physics, including not only the organism-complex, but also the whole complex of physical factors forming what we call the environment.

moments.takeaway: The 'ecosystem' replaces vaguer notions of community. Energy and matter flows can now be the unit of analysis.

moments.title: Lindeman's energy flow
moments.body:
Raymond Lindeman, working on his PhD at Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota, measures energy flow at each trophic level in the lake ecosystem. He shows that ecological efficiency drops by ~90% at each level — the basis of the 'ten percent rule'.

Lindeman dies of liver disease in 1942 aged 26, shortly after submitting his paper to Ecology. The paper is initially rejected. His advisor, G. Evelyn Hutchinson, fights for it. It is published posthumously and becomes the founding paper of quantitative ecosystem ecology.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative energy flow can be measured ecosystem-wide. Trophic structure has a thermodynamic explanation.

moments.title: Carson's Silent Spring
moments.body:
Rachel Carson publishes 'Silent Spring', documenting how DDT and other persistent pesticides accumulate up food chains, devastating bird populations (raptors with thin eggshells could not reproduce). She frames it as ecological warfare on the natural world.

The chemical industry attacks Carson personally. She testifies before Congress while terminally ill with breast cancer. DDT is banned in the US in 1972, 8 years after her death. The environmental movement begins.

quote.text: The 'control of nature' is a phrase conceived in arrogance, born of the Neanderthal age of biology and the convenience of man.

moments.takeaway: Public ecological awareness arrives in mainstream culture. Environmental regulation begins.

moments.title: MacArthur and Wilson — island biogeography
moments.who: Robert MacArthur (Princeton) and E. O. Wilson (Harvard)
moments.body:
MacArthur and Wilson publish 'The Theory of Island Biogeography', proposing that the number of species on an island reflects a balance between colonisation and extinction — both rate-dependent on island size and distance from mainland.

The theory makes quantitative predictions about species-area relationships that hold across taxa. It is later extended to fragmented habitats by Jared Diamond (1975), forming the theoretical basis of nature reserve design.
moments.takeaway: Ecology becomes mathematical. Species richness can be predicted from physical principles.

now.title: Ecology today
now.body:
Modern ecology is data-rich: satellite observations of global vegetation, eDNA for tracking species, automated acoustic monitoring, citizen science platforms (iNaturalist, eBird), and continental-scale experiments (NEON, FLUXNET).

Major focus areas: climate change ecology, conservation biology, biodiversity loss, ecological restoration, biogeochemical cycles, urban ecology, microbial ecology.
now.open_questions: What's the rate of contemporary species loss, and how do we slow it? How do we restore degraded ecosystems? What are the planetary boundaries (Rockström 2009) we cannot safely cross? Can ecosystem services (Costanza et al.) be valued and protected through markets? How do we communicate ecological complexity to policymakers?

items.reflection: Lindeman died at 26. Carson died at 56 from cancer, while being attacked by chemical companies as 'hysterical'. The founders of modern ecology often paid heavy personal prices. What does it cost to be early on environmental ideas the public is not yet ready to hear?

moments.title: MacArthur and Wilson formalise island biogeography
moments.who: Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson
moments.body:
Their book 'The Theory of Island Biogeography' proposes the equilibrium model: an island's species count reflects balance between immigration (decreasing with distance from mainland) and extinction (decreasing with island size).

The theory predicts species-area relationships (S = c * A^z, with z typically 0.2-0.3) that hold across many taxa and many island systems.
moments.takeaway: Ecology becomes quantitative and predictive. The rate of species discovery can be modelled.

moments.title: Simberloff and Wilson's mangrove experiment
moments.who: Daniel Simberloff and E. O. Wilson, Florida Keys
moments.body:
They fumigate small mangrove islands in the Florida Keys, killing all arthropods, then track recolonisation. The number of arthropod species returns to roughly its original value within a year — and depends on island size and distance from sources, as predicted.

The experiment is one of the first manipulative tests of an ecological theory at whole-ecosystem scale.
moments.takeaway: Theory makes a prediction. Experiment confirms it. Ecology can be predictive.

moments.title: Diamond and reserve design
moments.body:
Diamond publishes 'The Island Dilemma: Lessons of Modern Biogeographic Studies for the Design of Natural Reserves'. He proposes principles: bigger is better, fewer large reserves are better than many small ones (the 'SLOSS' debate — Single Large Or Several Small), corridors connecting reserves help, round shapes preferable to elongated.

The principles become standard in conservation planning, though the SLOSS question is still debated.
moments.takeaway: Conservation biology has theoretical foundations. Reserve design is no longer pure intuition.

moments.title: Wilson on biodiversity
moments.body:
Wilson popularises the term 'biodiversity' (the National Forum on BioDiversity, 1986) and emphasises the magnitude of the extinction crisis. He estimates 27,000 species go extinct yearly, largely undocumented insects in tropical forests.

His 1992 book 'The Diversity of Life' becomes a standard text. Wilson promotes the 'Half-Earth' proposal — setting aside half of Earth's surface for nature.
moments.takeaway: Biodiversity becomes a mainstream concept. The scale of contemporary loss is communicated to the public.

moments.title: Planetary boundaries and the sixth extinction
moments.body:
Johan Rockström and colleagues (2009) propose 'planetary boundaries' for nine Earth-system processes (climate, biodiversity, biogeochemical flows, etc.). They argue several have been crossed.

Ceballos, Ehrlich and Dirzo (2014, 2017) document accelerating vertebrate extinctions, framing the current epoch as the sixth mass extinction. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017) confirm losses extend across non-charismatic groups.
moments.takeaway: The biodiversity crisis is now a quantified, defended scientific consensus. Whether it's a 'mass extinction' depends on how the term is defined.

now.title: Biodiversity today
now.body:
Earth's species count is unknown — estimates range from 2 million to 100 million. Mora et al. (2011) estimate ~8.7 million eukaryotic species, of which ~1.5 million are described.

Protected areas now cover ~17% of land and ~8% of oceans. The post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework targets 30% by 2030 ('30x30').

Genomic tools (eDNA, metabarcoding) are revolutionising species detection. Citizen science (iNaturalist, eBird) generates billions of observations.
now.open_questions: How many species are there really? What's the rate of contemporary extinction? How do we conserve in a changing climate when species' ranges shift? Can de-extinction (CRISPR, IVF on cryopreserved tissue) restore lost species? What's the ethical status of species — is biodiversity loss intrinsically wrong, or only insofar as it harms humans?

items.reflection: E. O. Wilson worked on ants for most of his career and on biodiversity in his last decades. He was also at the centre of the sociobiology controversies of the 1970s, attacked from the political left. What is the responsibility of scientists to advocate for the implications of their research — and what happens when those implications challenge cherished political assumptions?

moments.title: Galen's two-system model
moments.body:
Galen proposes that blood is made in the liver from food, ebbs and flows in veins to nourish the body, and is consumed in tissues. Some blood passes through invisible pores in the heart's interventricular septum from right to left ventricle, mixes with 'pneuma' from the lungs, and is distributed in arteries.

No circulation. Blood is consumed; new blood is constantly made. This view dominates Western medicine for 1400 years.
moments.takeaway: A coherent but wrong model holds medical thought for over a millennium. Galen's authority is hard to challenge.

moments.title: Ibn al-Nafis describes pulmonary circulation
moments.body:
Ibn al-Nafis, a Syrian physician, writes a commentary on Avicenna's Canon of Medicine. He argues, based on anatomy, that blood cannot cross the septum directly: it must flow from right ventricle through lungs to left ventricle.

His text is preserved in Arabic but largely unknown to European medicine. Pulmonary circulation is rediscovered by Michael Servetus (1553, burned at the stake), Realdo Colombo (1559), and definitively by Harvey.
moments.takeaway: Pulmonary circulation is described 400 years before Harvey, in a tradition that doesn't reach Europe in time.

moments.title: Harvey's De Motu Cordis
moments.who: William Harvey, Royal College of Physicians, London
moments.body:
William Harvey publishes 'Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus' — the anatomical exercise on the motion of the heart and blood in animals. Based on quantitative anatomy:

- The heart's left ventricle holds ~2 oz of blood. Beats ~70/min. That's 8400 oz/hour — ~75 kg of blood per hour, far more than the body contains.
- Conclusion: blood cannot be continuously consumed. It must circulate, returning to the heart.
- Demonstrates with vein experiments: pressing veins shows blood flows from periphery to heart; valves prevent backflow.

quote.text: It is absolutely necessary to conclude that the blood in the animal body is impelled in a circle, and is in a state of ceaseless motion.

moments.takeaway: Quantitative reasoning settles a 1400-year-old anatomical question. Blood circulates.

moments.title: Malpighi sees capillaries
moments.body:
Harvey had reasoned that blood must connect arteries to veins via invisible vessels in the tissues. He never saw them — they were below the resolution of his time.

Marcello Malpighi, using one of the first practical microscopes, sees blood flowing through capillaries in a frog's lung in 1661. The capillary network is the missing link.
moments.takeaway: Microscopy completes Harvey's picture. Arteries connect to veins through capillary beds.

moments.title: Hales measures blood pressure
moments.body:
Stephen Hales, an English clergyman and physiologist, inserts a long glass tube into the artery of a restrained horse. Blood rises in the tube to about 8 feet. Hales has measured blood pressure for the first time.

The measurement confirms that blood is under significant pressure in arteries — supporting Harvey's pump model. Hales also measures cardiac output and root pressure in plants. He works at the intersection of physics and physiology.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative physiology arrives. Pressures, volumes and flows can be measured directly.

now.title: Cardiovascular physiology today
now.body:
We understand the heart at every level: ion channels, conduction system, mechanics, hormonal control, regenerative limits. Echocardiography images live hearts. Cardiac catheterisation accesses coronary arteries through wrist or groin punctures.

Major advances: coronary artery bypass grafting (1960s), heart transplantation (Barnard 1967), implantable pacemakers (Bakken/Lillehei 1958), stents (1986), ECMO life support, CRISPR-based gene therapy for inherited cardiomyopathies.
now.open_questions: Can heart muscle be made to regenerate after infarction? Why doesn't normal mammalian heart muscle regenerate the way zebrafish heart does? What's the molecular basis of sudden cardiac death? Can we predict who is at risk of cardiovascular events using genomics and wearable monitoring?

items.reflection: Harvey faced ridicule for overturning Galen. Servetus was burned for it. Ibn al-Nafis was forgotten. Hales was a clergyman doing measurements no one had thought to make. Each step took different kinds of courage: against authority, against orthodoxy, against the limits of available technology. Which kind of barrier is hardest to break?

moments.title: Golgi invents the black reaction
moments.body:
Camillo Golgi develops the 'reazione nera' (black reaction): a silver nitrate impregnation that, randomly, stains a small fraction of neurons completely black against a clear background — revealing their full morphology for the first time.

Golgi himself, looking at his own preparations, concludes that the brain is a continuous reticular network, with nerve cells forming a single syncytium.
moments.takeaway: Brain microanatomy becomes visible. The stain is excellent. The interpretation is wrong.

moments.title: Cajal and the neuron doctrine
moments.body:
Santiago Ramón y Cajal, a Spanish histologist who modified Golgi's method, examines hundreds of brain regions in many species. He concludes the opposite of Golgi: nerve cells are individual, separate units, contacting each other but not continuous.

The 'neuron doctrine': the nervous system is built of discrete neurons that communicate at points of contact (later named synapses by Sherrington, 1897).

Cajal and Golgi share the 1906 Nobel Prize — and use their Nobel lectures to attack each other's interpretations. Cajal is right; Golgi cannot accept it.

quote.text: Nothing inspires more reverence and awe in me than an old man who knows how to change his mind.

moments.takeaway: Same data, opposite interpretations. Cajal's neuron doctrine becomes the foundation of modern neuroscience.

moments.title: Cole and Curtis measure membrane impedance
moments.who: Kenneth Cole and Howard Curtis, Woods Hole
moments.body: Cole and Curtis show that during an action potential, the squid giant axon's membrane impedance drops sharply — implying ion channels open transiently. The action potential is an electrochemical event, not a chemical wave.
moments.takeaway: The action potential involves rapid changes in membrane permeability. The biophysics of nerve firing is now experimentally tractable.

moments.title: Hodgkin and Huxley — the action potential
moments.who: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley, Plymouth and Cambridge
moments.body:
Hodgkin and Huxley use the giant axon of the squid Loligo (up to 1 mm diameter — easy to put electrodes in) to dissect the action potential. They develop the voltage-clamp technique, measure separate Na+ and K+ currents, and write a set of differential equations that describe the action potential mathematically.

Their equations predict the timing and shape of action potentials with remarkable accuracy. They share the 1963 Nobel Prize with John Eccles (who worked out synaptic transmission).

quote.text: The chief object of these experiments was to find equations which described the conductances with reasonable accuracy and were sufficiently simple for theoretical calculation of the action potential.

moments.takeaway: The action potential is a mathematical object. Biology gets a piece of physics it could not previously match.

moments.title: Patch clamp and the single channel
moments.who: Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann, Göttingen
moments.body:
Neher and Sakmann develop the patch clamp technique: a glass pipette with a tiny opening forms a high-resistance seal with a small patch of cell membrane, allowing the current through a SINGLE ion channel to be measured.

Ion channels — predicted by Hodgkin and Huxley but never seen — are now observable as individual molecules switching between open and closed states. Neher and Sakmann share the 1991 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The molecular components of the nervous system are now individually measurable in real time.

now.title: Neuroscience today
now.body:
We have functional MRI, two-photon microscopy of live cortex, optogenetic control of specific neurons, transcriptomics of individual cells. Connectomics is mapping every synapse in small brains (C. elegans done; Drosophila in progress). Brain-computer interfaces are restoring movement to paralysed patients.

Still, the brain remains one of science's great frontiers. Even C. elegans (302 neurons, full wiring diagram since 1986) is not fully understood behaviourally.
now.open_questions: How does the brain compute? What is consciousness, and which (if any) brain structures are necessary or sufficient for it? Can we treat depression, Alzheimer's, schizophrenia at their neural causes? Can we map a mammalian brain completely? Are large AI models doing 'thinking' in any neurobiologically relevant sense?

items.reflection: Cajal and Golgi shared a Nobel Prize for results that contradicted each other. Cajal was right but never spoke ill of Golgi. Golgi never accepted his rival's interpretation. How does science handle situations where rival theories are honoured together, and how should we treat scientists whose right ideas overturned the work of those they admired?

moments.title: Payen and Persoz isolate the first enzyme
moments.who: Anselme Payen and Jean-François Persoz, Paris
moments.body:
Payen and Persoz extract a substance from malt that converts starch to sugar. They call it 'diastase' (from Greek 'separation'). Diastase is what we now call amylase.

It's a particular substance with a particular activity, isolated from a biological source — the first recognised enzyme.
moments.takeaway: Specific catalysts can be extracted from biological materials. The concept of an 'enzyme' is born.

moments.title: Pasteur and vitalism
moments.body:
Pasteur, asked to investigate problems in sugar beet fermentation, shows that fermentation is caused by living yeast cells. He argues that life is essential — there is something 'vital' in living cells that cannot be reduced to chemistry.

This vitalist position dominates 19th-century biology and seems strongly supported by Pasteur's work.
moments.takeaway: Pasteur defends a vitalist view: only living cells can ferment. The position seems empirically secure.

moments.title: Buchner's cell-free fermentation
moments.body:
Eduard Buchner grinds yeast with sand and diatomaceous earth, presses the mush, filters out all cell debris. The clear yellow liquid (called 'press juice') ferments sugar just like live yeast.

No living cells. Just biochemical extracts. Fermentation does not require life — it requires enzymes. Vitalism is wrong.

Buchner wins the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He dies in WWI in 1917, hit by shrapnel at the Eastern Front.

quote.text: We are seeing the cells of yeast more and more clearly as a chemical machine.

moments.takeaway: Life is chemistry. Vitalism collapses. Biochemistry as a discipline can begin.

moments.title: Sumner crystallises an enzyme
moments.body:
James Sumner crystallises urease (an enzyme that breaks down urea) from jack beans. He shows the crystals are pure protein and retain enzymatic activity.

The finding is controversial — many biochemists had assumed enzymes were 'colloidal' or 'living'. By the late 1930s, enzymes are accepted as proteins. Sumner shares the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Northrop and Wendell Stanley.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are proteins. They can be crystallised, purified, characterised — they are chemicals, not mysterious life-substances.

moments.title: Koshland's induced fit
moments.body:
Koshland refines Emil Fischer's 1894 'lock and key' model with induced fit: the active site of an enzyme is not pre-formed but molded by the substrate as it binds. This explains why enzymes are flexible and how subtle structural changes regulate catalysis.

Linus Pauling's 1948 insight — that enzymes catalyse by binding transition states — supplements both models.
moments.takeaway: Enzyme catalysis is dynamic, not static. The shape of the active site is part of the chemistry.

now.title: Enzymology today
now.body:
We have atomic-resolution structures of thousands of enzymes (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM). AlphaFold (2021) predicts structures from sequence alone. We engineer enzymes for industrial use, design new catalysts for reactions nature never invented, and understand most major catalytic mechanisms.

Applications: detergents (proteases, lipases), food processing, biofuels, pharmaceuticals, plastic degradation (PET hydrolases for recycling), DNA manipulation tools.
now.open_questions: Can we design enzymes from scratch to catalyse any desired reaction? Can we make enzymes work in harsh industrial conditions? What's the role of dynamics (not just structure) in catalysis? Are there entire enzyme classes we haven't discovered?

items.reflection: Pasteur was so confident in vitalism that he resisted the implications of his own century's chemistry. Buchner's accidental experiment overturned his teacher's worldview. Sumner crystallised urease in conditions colleagues called 'foolish'. How often do major paradigm shifts depend on someone willing to try the experiment that the consensus declares unnecessary?

moments.title: Darwin and his son work out plant signalling
moments.who: Charles and Francis Darwin, Down House, Kent
moments.body:
In 'The Power of Movement in Plants' (1880), Charles Darwin and his son Francis show that grass coleoptiles bend toward light because the TIP senses the light, but the bending happens lower down. They cover the tip with foil — no bending. They cover the lower part — bending still occurs.

The Darwins conclude that some signal must travel from tip to bending region. They have discovered plant hormonal signalling without knowing the chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Darwin's last book describes plant signalling decades before the molecule responsible is identified.

moments.title: Boysen-Jensen — chemical signal
moments.body:
Boysen-Jensen places a thin agar block between a coleoptile tip and the lower regions. The signal still passes — plants bend normally. He repeats with mica (impermeable): no bending.

The signal is chemical, not electrical or neural. It diffuses through agar but not through inert mica.
moments.takeaway: The plant 'signal' is a chemical that diffuses through water.

moments.title: Went isolates auxin
moments.body:
Frits Went collects the signal in agar blocks placed beneath cut coleoptile tips, then applies the loaded blocks asymmetrically to decapitated coleoptiles. The headless plants bend — the chemical alone is sufficient to cause growth.

Went names the compound 'auxin' (Greek 'to grow'). It takes another decade to identify it chemically as indole-3-acetic acid (IAA).
moments.takeaway: The signal can be transferred between plants in agar. Plant growth has a chemical messenger.

moments.title: Other plant hormones
moments.who: Various — including Kurosawa, Yabuta, Skoog, Miller
moments.body:
Gibberellins (Kurosawa 1926, Yabuta 1935) — first identified as the cause of 'foolish seedling disease' in rice. Promote stem elongation.

Cytokinins (Skoog and Miller, 1955) — promote cell division in tissue culture; balance with auxin determines shoot vs root formation.

Abscisic acid (Addicott, 1963) — promotes leaf drop, seed dormancy, stomatal closure in drought.

Ethylene (Neljubow, 1901; later confirmed) — gaseous hormone that ripens fruit and triggers leaf abscission.

Five major hormone classes — auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, ABA, ethylene — control most of plant growth and development. Later additions: brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid, strigolactones.
moments.takeaway: Plants run an integrated hormonal communication network with at least a dozen major messenger molecules.

moments.title: Receptors and transcription
moments.body:
Auxin receptor (TIR1) identified 2005. Gibberellin receptor (GID1) 2005. ABA receptor (PYR/PYL/RCAR) 2009. Each hormone signals through specific receptor proteins to alter gene expression.

Molecular plant biology is now as detailed as molecular animal biology. We can engineer plants with altered hormone signalling for agricultural traits.
moments.takeaway: Plant signal transduction is fully molecular. Receptors and downstream networks are known for each hormone.

now.title: Plant hormones today
now.body:
Hormones are deployed agriculturally: ethylene (banana ripening), gibberellins (sprouting promotion), auxin analogues (rooting hormones, herbicides like 2,4-D — selective for broadleaf weeds), cytokinins (cell culture).

Climate change is driving research on stress hormones (especially ABA). Drought-resistant crops often involve altered ABA signalling.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer crops with optimised hormonal balance for higher yields, stress tolerance, smaller stature (the green revolution achieved this for some grains)? What's the full crosstalk between hormone systems? Are there undiscovered plant hormones?

items.reflection: Darwin wrote about plant signalling 75 years before its chemical basis was identified. He correctly inferred that something must travel; he had no way to know what. How much of biology has been correctly inferred long before the molecular details became available — and how does this kind of 'theoretical biology' get done well?

moments.title: Scheele and Priestley discover oxygen
moments.who: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (Sweden) and Joseph Priestley (England) — independently
moments.body:
Scheele isolates 'fire air' (oxygen) around 1772 by heating various metal oxides. His findings are published in 1777, delayed by his publisher.

Priestley independently isolates the same gas in 1774 by focusing sunlight onto mercuric oxide. He notes that a candle burns more brightly in it and a mouse can live longer. He calls it 'dephlogisticated air' — fitting his (incorrect) phlogiston theory.
moments.takeaway: A new gas is isolated. Both discoverers interpret it within frameworks soon to be discarded.

moments.title: Lavoisier explains combustion as oxidation
moments.body:
Priestley meets Lavoisier in Paris in 1774 and tells him of the gas. Lavoisier names it 'oxygène' (acid-former), proposes that combustion is union of substances with oxygen (not loss of 'phlogiston'), and overturns the phlogiston theory.

Lavoisier shows that respiration is essentially slow combustion — animals breathe in oxygen, breathe out CO2, and the same proportions hold as for burning charcoal. His quantitative experiments inaugurate modern chemistry.

quote.text: Respiration is therefore a combustion, very slow it is true, but otherwise perfectly similar to that of charcoal.

moments.takeaway: Animal respiration is chemistry. Burning food in the body explains body heat and waste gases.

moments.title: Lavoisier executed
moments.who: Lavoisier, Place de la Révolution, Paris
moments.body:
Lavoisier, as a former tax farmer under the ancien régime, is guillotined during the Terror. The judge reportedly says 'The Republic has no need of scientists.' His friend Lagrange laments: 'It took them only an instant to cut off his head, but France may not produce another such head in a century.'

Lavoisier is 50. His widow, Marie-Anne Paulze (a chemist herself, who illustrated his books and translated chemical texts), preserves his papers.
moments.takeaway: Founding modern chemistry doesn't protect you from politics.

moments.title: Liebig and animal chemistry
moments.body:
Liebig extends Lavoisier's view: foods can be classified by what they're oxidised to. Carbohydrates and fats are 'respiratory' (oxidised for heat). Proteins are 'plastic' (build tissue, sometimes oxidised for energy too).

Liebig also (incorrectly) believes plant carbon comes from soil humus — wrong, but his fertilizer chemistry transforms agriculture.
moments.takeaway: Food chemistry begins. Macronutrients are classified by metabolic fate.

moments.title: Krebs cycle
moments.body:
Hans Krebs, having fled Nazi Germany, works out the cycle of reactions by which acetyl groups are oxidised to CO2 with the reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reactions are eight; the substrate (citrate) lends its name.

The cycle takes place in mitochondria. Together with electron transport, it represents the bulk of aerobic ATP production. Krebs wins the 1953 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The chemistry of cellular respiration is mapped reaction by reaction. Lavoisier's 'slow combustion' is now an enzymatic cycle.

now.title: Respiration today
now.body:
Aerobic respiration is mapped from glucose to ATP at atomic resolution. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in many diseases. We can measure cellular oxygen consumption in real time (Seahorse extracellular flux analysers) to phenotype metabolism.
