Applications: mitochondrial medicine, exercise physiology, sports science, aging research, drug screening.
now.open_questions: What aspect of mitochondrial decline causes aging? Can we therapeutically boost mitochondrial biogenesis? Why are some mutations in oxidative phosphorylation genes tolerated while others are lethal? How does metabolic flexibility (switching between fuels) work mechanistically?

items.reflection: Lavoisier was executed for being a tax collector. Priestley fled to America after Birmingham mobs burned down his lab for his support of the French Revolution. Krebs fled Germany. Buchner died at the Eastern Front. The biochemistry of respiration was developed by people whose lives were constantly disrupted by political and military violence. What does science achieve in spite of, and what does it lose to, history?

moments.title: Linnaeus publishes Systema Naturae
moments.body:
Carl Linnaeus, a 28-year-old Swedish botanist, publishes the first edition of Systema Naturae — a tabular classification of the three 'kingdoms' (animal, vegetable, mineral). It's 11 pages long.

Over 12 editions, it grows to ~3000 pages. The 10th edition (1758) is the modern starting point for animal nomenclature. Linnaeus introduces binomial nomenclature: every species gets two names (genus and species) — a system still used.
moments.takeaway: A young botanist invents a classification system that lasts for centuries.

moments.title: Apostles and species discovery
moments.body:
Linnaeus sends students (his 'apostles') around the world to collect specimens. Daniel Solander travels with Cook to Australia. Pehr Kalm travels in North America. Several die on their expeditions (Bjornstahl in Cyprus, Forsskal in Yemen, Hasselquist in Smyrna).

The apostles bring back thousands of new species. Linnaeus describes them all in subsequent editions. The number of described species grows rapidly.
moments.takeaway: Biological classification becomes a global enterprise. Apostles pay heavy personal costs for natural history.

moments.title: Darwin gives classification an evolutionary basis
moments.body:
Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) reframes taxonomy. Categories are no longer arbitrary divisions — they reflect descent. Species in the same genus share a recent common ancestor; species in the same family a more remote one. Classification becomes phylogenetic.

Darwin: 'Our classifications will come to be, as far as they can be so made, genealogies.'
moments.takeaway: Classification has a biological meaning. Tree-shaped descent maps onto the hierarchical categories.

moments.title: Five kingdoms
moments.body:
Whittaker proposes a five-kingdom system: Monera (bacteria), Protista (single-celled eukaryotes), Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. The system distinguishes prokaryotes from eukaryotes and separates fungi from plants.

Margaret Dayhoff's 1965 molecular sequences begin to provide an alternative classifier — molecular phylogeny. Carl Woese will soon use ribosomal RNA to redraw the deepest branches.
moments.takeaway: Higher-level classification reflects fundamental cellular differences.

moments.title: Woese discovers archaea
moments.body:
Carl Woese sequences 16S ribosomal RNA across many organisms. He finds that some 'bacteria' (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles) are as different from other bacteria as from eukaryotes. He proposes a third domain: Archaea.

The tree of life now has THREE domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) rather than two kingdoms (prokaryote vs eukaryote). Eukaryotes appear most closely related to archaea, especially as nuclear ancestry — consistent with later endosymbiotic theory.
moments.takeaway: Molecular phylogenetics rewrites the deepest divisions of life. Three domains, not two.

now.title: Taxonomy today
now.body:
Molecular phylogenetics dominates. Whole-genome trees, single-gene trees, and metagenomic sequences from environmental samples constantly reshape our view of life.

Most named species (over 1.5 million) are still based on morphology. eDNA and high-throughput sequencing are revealing huge diversity of microbes (CPR bacteria, Asgard archaea — the latter likely the closest archaeal relatives of eukaryotes).
now.open_questions: How many species are there? How do we name species we've only seen as DNA sequences? What were the deepest divergences in the tree of life, and when did they occur? Where do viruses fit (they aren't on the tree in any standard sense)?

items.reflection: Linnaeus considered humans (Homo sapiens) part of order Primates. This was controversial — he was placing humans in nature, not above it. Two centuries later, Darwin made the connection explicit, and a century after that, DNA showed humans share 98% of their genome with chimps. How has the taxonomic placing of humans alongside other animals shaped — slowly, contentiously — what we think we are?

moments.title: Bernal and Crowfoot — first protein crystal X-ray pattern
moments.who: J. D. Bernal and Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin, Cambridge
moments.body:
Bernal and his student Dorothy Crowfoot obtain the first X-ray diffraction pattern of a protein crystal (pepsin). It shows that proteins have defined three-dimensional structures with regular features.

Crowfoot Hodgkin will go on to solve penicillin (1945), vitamin B12 (1956), and insulin (1969), winning the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Proteins are not amorphous. They have defined structures, which X-ray crystallography can in principle reveal.

moments.title: Pauling proposes the alpha helix
moments.who: Linus Pauling and Robert Corey, Caltech
moments.body:
Pauling and Corey work out the geometry of polypeptide chains, allowing for hydrogen bonding. They predict that proteins should commonly contain an alpha helix and a beta sheet. They build the helix using paper models, in bed while Pauling has flu.

They publish before any X-ray data confirms it. Within months, model and data match.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical chemistry predicts protein structural motifs from first principles. Experimentation confirms.

moments.title: Kendrew solves myoglobin
moments.body:
John Kendrew, working at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, solves the structure of sperm whale myoglobin — the oxygen-storage protein of muscle. The first three-dimensional protein structure.

The structure looks ugly: an asymmetric tangle with no obvious symmetry. Pauling had hoped for elegance; he gets a 'visceral lump'. But it's REAL.

quote.text: Perhaps the most striking features of the molecule are its complexity and its lack of symmetry. The arrangement seems to be almost totally lacking in the kind of regularities which one instinctively anticipates.

moments.takeaway: The first protein structure is irregular. Functional sophistication arises from specific, asymmetric folds — not from neat geometry.

moments.title: Perutz solves hemoglobin
moments.body:
Max Perutz, after 22 years of work, solves the structure of hemoglobin. He shares the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Kendrew.

Hemoglobin is four similar subunits, each like myoglobin. Perutz later works out the structural changes during oxygen binding — the molecular basis of cooperative binding (T state vs R state).
moments.takeaway: Multi-subunit proteins are now structurally accessible. Conformational changes drive function.

moments.title: AlphaFold
moments.body:
DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicts protein structures from sequence with accuracy comparable to experimental methods. The 'protein folding problem' — predicting structure from sequence — had been considered one of biology's biggest unsolved problems.

The AlphaFold database (2022) contains predicted structures for ~200 million proteins — essentially all known proteins. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to John Jumper, Demis Hassabis (AlphaFold) and David Baker (de novo protein design).
moments.takeaway: An AI system effectively solves a 50-year-old central problem of biochemistry. Most known proteins now have a predicted structure.

now.title: Protein structure today
now.body:
We have experimental structures for ~200,000 proteins and predicted structures for ~200 million. Cryo-EM (single-particle) is now solving structures at near-atomic resolution without crystallisation. AlphaFold and related tools predict effects of mutations, ligand binding, design new proteins.

Applications: structure-based drug design (almost all modern drug discovery), enzyme engineering, vaccine design, understanding genetic disease.
now.open_questions: How do proteins fold dynamically (the kinetic, not just final, problem)? Can we design proteins with novel functions reliably? How do disordered proteins work? What happens when proteins misfold (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's)?

items.reflection: Kendrew's first structure was ugly. Many later structures are not 'beautiful' by Pauling's standard either. Beauty in biology emerges at a higher level — the function works, not because the shape is symmetric, but because asymmetric details position atoms exactly where chemistry needs them. How often is our aesthetic intuition a poor guide to scientific reality?

moments.title: Van Leeuwenhoek sees his own dental plaque
moments.body:
Van Leeuwenhoek, the Delft draper and microscopy hobbyist, looks at scrapings of his own teeth under his single-lens microscopes. He sees swarming 'animalcules'. He writes to the Royal Society describing the diverse bacteria of human dental plaque — the first observation of human microbiota.

He also notes that vinegar kills many of them on contact.
moments.takeaway: Three centuries ago, microbes in the human body were observed. Their significance took most of that time to be appreciated.

moments.title: Escherich isolates E. coli
moments.body:
Theodor Escherich isolates and characterises the bacterium that comes to bear his name (Escherichia coli) from infant stool. It becomes the most-studied bacterium in biology — model organism for genetics, biochemistry, and microbiology.

E. coli is one of trillions of bacterial cells in the human gut. The full diversity of the gut microbiome takes another century to begin mapping.
moments.takeaway: Specific human gut bacteria can be cultured and studied. Most can't be — they need their natural community.

moments.title: Gnotobiotic mice
moments.who: Phil Trexler and colleagues, Lobund Institute (Notre Dame)
moments.body:
Researchers raise mice in completely sterile conditions ('germ-free' or gnotobiotic). They show that without bacteria, mice have abnormal immune systems, altered gut development, behavioural changes, and resistance to certain diseases.

Gnotobiotic models become essential tools for understanding the role of microbiota in health.
moments.takeaway: Microbes are not optional inhabitants — they shape the host's biology fundamentally.

moments.title: Human Microbiome Project
moments.body:
The Human Microbiome Project sequences bacteria from healthy volunteers at multiple body sites using 16S ribosomal RNA gene amplification and metagenomics. It reveals enormous diversity: ~10,000+ species in the gut alone, with substantial inter-individual variation.

The European MetaHIT project runs in parallel. Together they establish baselines for healthy human microbiomes and frame disease-associated alterations ('dysbiosis').
moments.takeaway: Human microbiomes are quantitatively defined. Disease patterns can be looked for against a baseline.

moments.title: Faecal microbiota transplant becomes clinical
moments.body:
FMT for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection is shown effective in randomised trials (van Nood et al., 2013): ~90% cure rate vs ~30% for standard antibiotics. FMT becomes accepted clinical practice for refractory C. difficile.

Trials for other conditions (ulcerative colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, metabolic syndrome, neurodegenerative diseases) are ongoing, with mixed results. The FDA approved two FMT-derived products in 2022-23 (Rebyota, Vowst).
moments.takeaway: Restoring a healthy gut community can cure a stubborn disease. The microbiome is now therapeutic.

now.title: Microbiome today
now.body:
Microbiome research is a major scientific field. We have rich catalogues of gut, skin, oral, vaginal and respiratory microbiomes. Specific bacteria are linked to autoimmune disease, obesity, depression, drug responses.

Industry: probiotic products, personalised microbiome diagnostics, microbe-targeted drugs, faecal transplant capsules.
now.open_questions: Causal effects of microbiome on disease? (Mostly correlations so far.) What are the rules of microbial community assembly? Can we engineer microbiomes for specific outcomes? What's the role of bacteriophages, fungi and protists in the microbiome (mostly understudied)?

items.reflection: Van Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria in his teeth in 1683. The first hint that they MATTER to human health came centuries later. The full appreciation of the microbiome as a quasi-organ is barely two decades old. How often does science have the evidence but not the framework to recognise importance — and what other 'obvious' things are we still failing to recognise?

moments.title: Tyndall measures CO2 absorption
moments.body:
John Tyndall builds an apparatus to measure how much infrared radiation different gases absorb. He finds nitrogen and oxygen (~99% of the atmosphere) are essentially transparent to IR. Water vapour, CO2 and ozone strongly absorb.

He correctly identifies these as 'greenhouse gases' that warm the planet by absorbing emitted IR. He doesn't predict that human emissions will matter — but he provides the physics.
moments.takeaway: The greenhouse effect is identified experimentally 160 years before the policy debate.

moments.title: Arrhenius calculates CO2 warming
moments.body:
Svante Arrhenius — a chemist who also won the Nobel for the dissociation of electrolytes — calculates the temperature change from doubling atmospheric CO2. Without computers. By hand, over a year.

He estimates 5-6 C warming. Modern estimates are 2.5-4 C — Arrhenius was a bit high but right in magnitude and direction. He optimistically thought the warming would benefit Sweden.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative climate sensitivity is calculated in 1896. The numbers are not far from modern estimates.

moments.title: Callendar links CO2 to warming
moments.body:
Guy Callendar, an English steam engineer with meteorological interests, presents evidence to the Royal Meteorological Society: atmospheric CO2 has risen ~10% in 50 years (due to fossil fuel burning), and global temperatures have warmed by about 0.3 C over the same period.

He correctly identifies anthropogenic CO2 as the cause. His paper is largely dismissed at the time.
moments.takeaway: Anthropogenic warming is observed and attributed in 1938. Most scientists initially disagree.

moments.title: Keeling at Mauna Loa
moments.who: Charles David Keeling, Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii
moments.body:
Charles Keeling starts continuous CO2 measurements at Mauna Loa in 1958. The 'Keeling Curve' shows annual seasonal variation (vegetation breathing in northern summer) superimposed on a relentless upward trend.

CO2 in 1958: 315 ppm. In 2024: 425 ppm. Pre-industrial: ~280 ppm. The most famous chart in environmental science. Keeling's son Ralph continues the measurements after Charles's death in 2005.

quote.text: If we are heading for trouble, we ought to know it.
quote.attrib: Charles David Keeling, on starting the Mauna Loa measurements

moments.takeaway: Continuous, precise measurement turns climate change from speculation into observation. The Keeling Curve becomes irrefutable.

moments.title: IPCC and policy
moments.who: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, multiple
moments.body:
The IPCC, established 1988, synthesises climate science across thousands of papers and authors. The First Assessment Report (1990) led to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992). The Paris Agreement (2015) sets goals of limiting warming to 1.5-2 C above pre-industrial.

AR6 (2021-2023) reports unambiguous human attribution and accelerating impacts. Implementation lags ambition.
moments.takeaway: Climate science is institutionalised and globalised. Policy responses follow more slowly.

now.title: Climate science today
now.body:
We track CO2 at hundreds of stations. Satellites measure global temperature, ice cover, sea level. Climate models are sophisticated coupled atmosphere-ocean-biosphere simulations. Attribution science can now identify human influence in specific extreme weather events.

Known: 1.3 C warmer than pre-industrial; sea level rising ~3.6 mm/year; Arctic sea ice shrinking; ocean acidifying; glaciers retreating; ecosystems shifting.
now.open_questions: Climate sensitivity (the exact warming per CO2 doubling)? Tipping points (West Antarctic ice sheet, Amazon dieback, AMOC slowdown)? Cloud feedbacks? Aerosol forcing? Can we deploy carbon removal at scale? Solar geoengineering — ethics and risks?

items.reflection: Tyndall measured greenhouse absorption in 1859. Arrhenius calculated warming in 1896. Callendar attributed observed warming in 1938. Keeling started continuous monitoring in 1958. The IPCC formed in 1988. And major policy response is still incomplete in 2026. The physics has been understood for 165 years. What does this tell us about the relationship between scientific knowledge and political action?

moments.title: Gurdon shows differentiation is reversible
moments.body:
John Gurdon, a 28-year-old PhD student, transplants the nucleus of an adult frog intestinal cell into an enucleated frog egg. The egg develops into a full tadpole. The nucleus contains all the genetic information needed to make a whole animal — even after differentiation.

Gurdon's PhD supervisor had told him as a schoolboy that the idea of pursuing science was 'quite ridiculous'. Gurdon wins the Nobel Prize 50 years later, in 2012.
moments.takeaway: Differentiated cells retain the full genome. Specialisation is not loss of information — it's regulation of expression.

moments.title: Embryonic stem cells from mice
moments.who: Martin Evans and Matt Kaufman (Cambridge), Gail Martin (UCSF)
moments.body:
Two groups, independently, isolate pluripotent stem cells from mouse blastocysts and grow them in culture. The cells can be differentiated into any cell type. They can also be transferred back into early embryos to contribute to all tissues (chimeric mice).

Martin Evans goes on to develop gene targeting with embryonic stem cells (Nobel 2007).
moments.takeaway: Pluripotent cells can be cultured indefinitely. Stem cell research becomes possible.

moments.title: Human embryonic stem cells
moments.body:
James Thomson derives the first human embryonic stem cell lines from blastocysts donated by IVF clinics. The cells are pluripotent — they can differentiate into any human cell type.

The achievement is politically controversial. Federal funding restrictions are imposed in the US, lifted only in 2009. Research continues internationally.
moments.takeaway: Human pluripotent stem cells are available. Therapeutic applications are imagined.

moments.title: Yamanaka — induced pluripotent stem cells
moments.body:
Shinya Yamanaka shows that adult skin cells can be reprogrammed to pluripotent state by introducing just four genes (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc — the 'Yamanaka factors'). The resulting induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) behave essentially like embryonic stem cells.

Yamanaka and Gurdon share the 2012 Nobel Prize. iPSCs sidestep the ethical concerns of embryonic stem cell research.

quote.text: I started this work because I wanted to help patients with intractable diseases. I'm a doctor.

moments.takeaway: Four genes can turn any cell into a stem cell. The ethical and political restraints on stem cell research are partly bypassed.

moments.title: Stem cell therapies arrive
moments.body:
First iPSC-derived clinical trial: macular degeneration (Masayo Takahashi, Japan, 2014). The first patient's vision stabilised; second-patient trial was paused over a mutation concern. Progress is now wide: Parkinson's (iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons), spinal cord injury, type 1 diabetes (insulin-producing cells from iPSCs or ESCs, with Vertex's VX-880 showing first patient cures of insulin-dependent diabetes in 2022).

Many approved 'stem cell clinics' offer unproven treatments. The FDA has taken enforcement actions.
moments.takeaway: iPSC-derived therapies begin reaching patients. The promise of regenerative medicine is starting to be realised, slowly.

now.title: Stem cells today
now.body:
iPSC technology is standard. Lab-grown organoids (mini-brain, mini-gut, mini-kidney) model human development and disease. CRISPR-corrected iPSCs from patients are used for personalised drug testing and possibly autologous transplants.

Major areas: macular degeneration, Parkinson's, spinal injury, diabetes, heart failure. Drug screening using iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes catches cardiac toxicity before clinical trials.
now.open_questions: Can we reliably differentiate iPSCs into the specific cell types we need? Will iPSC-derived tissue evade immune rejection? Can we grow whole organs for transplant? What's the risk of tumours from incompletely differentiated cells? How do we regulate the 'stem cell clinic' market?

items.reflection: Gurdon's PhD supervisor told him science was 'quite ridiculous'. Yamanaka was a struggling orthopaedic surgeon who switched to research because he wasn't a good surgeon. Both eventually won Nobel Prizes that transformed biology and medicine. How do we identify and support the kinds of people who will succeed in research, when the most successful often look unlikely early on?

moments.title: Oparin and Haldane — primordial soup
moments.who: Alexander Oparin (Moscow) and J. B. S. Haldane (Cambridge) — independently
moments.body:
Both propose that early Earth's atmosphere was reducing (rich in hydrogen, methane, ammonia, water vapour), and that simple organic molecules could form spontaneously from these gases under ultraviolet light and lightning.

The resulting 'primordial soup' would contain amino acids, sugars, nucleotides. Over time, self-replicating molecules would emerge — and life would begin.
moments.takeaway: Life can in principle emerge from non-life. The hypothesis is articulated; it needs testing.

moments.title: Miller-Urey experiment
moments.who: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey, University of Chicago
moments.body:
Stanley Miller, a 23-year-old graduate student, builds a closed-loop apparatus with water (representing oceans), methane, ammonia and hydrogen (representing the atmosphere), with electric sparks (representing lightning). He runs it for a week.

The water turns brown. Analysis: 11 amino acids form, including alanine and glycine — the building blocks of proteins. From simple gases, simple chemistry under realistic conditions makes biology's monomers.

quote.text: Just turn on the spark and wait.

moments.takeaway: Building blocks of life form spontaneously under plausible early-Earth conditions.

moments.title: RNA world
moments.who: Walter Gilbert (Harvard), and others; Cech and Altman discover ribozymes
moments.body:
Thomas Cech (Colorado) and Sidney Altman (Yale) independently discover ribozymes — RNA molecules with catalytic activity (1982-83, Nobel 1989). RNA can both carry information AND catalyse reactions.

Walter Gilbert coins 'RNA world' (1986) for an early life stage where RNA did both jobs — predating DNA (better at information storage) and protein (better at catalysis). Modern ribosomes are essentially huge ribozymes — a vestige.
moments.takeaway: RNA can be both gene and enzyme. The RNA world is a plausible precursor to current biology.

moments.title: Hydrothermal vents
moments.body:
Submarine expeditions discover hydrothermal vents in the deep ocean. Bacterial communities live without sunlight, oxidising hydrogen sulfide from the vents. They support tubeworms, mussels, crabs — a complete ecosystem powered by Earth's interior, not the sun.

Mike Russell and Bill Martin propose (1990s-2000s) that life began at alkaline hydrothermal vents, where natural pH gradients across rocky mineral walls could have powered the first metabolism — like primitive ATP synthase machines.
moments.takeaway: Life can exist without sunlight. The origin of life may have been at hydrothermal vents — and proton gradients may have been the first energy source.

moments.title: LUCA and the tree of life
moments.who: Carl Woese, Bill Martin, Madeline Weiss and others
moments.body:
Sequencing extensive sets of universal genes (those present in all known life) yields a picture of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA). LUCA was likely a thermophile, anaerobe, that lived around hydrothermal vents about 4 billion years ago, used H2 and CO2 for metabolism, and had ribosomes already.

Weiss et al. (2016) identified ~355 genes likely present in LUCA. Life's deepest features — DNA-based information, RNA translation, ATP-based energy currency, lipid membranes — were already in place.
moments.takeaway: LUCA had most of modern biochemistry. The first life that gave rise to all known life was already complex. The earlier history is hidden.

now.title: Origin of life today
now.body:
Origin of life research has many threads: prebiotic chemistry (forming nucleotides from simple precursors — Sutherland's 2009 cyclic phosphate route), protocell assembly (Szostak's lab), RNA evolution in test tubes, alkaline vent geochemistry, ribosome evolution.

The Mars perseverance rover collects samples that may bear evidence of past microbial life. Europa, Enceladus and Titan are candidate sites for present-day life elsewhere.
now.open_questions: How did the first self-replicator arise? RNA, peptide, or both? Where (vent, pond, surface)? Could life have originated more than once on Earth (we'd never know — it would have been outcompeted)? Are we alone in the universe? What's the prebiotic plausibility of the genetic code's particular structure?

items.reflection: Origin of life is the most fundamental and least tractable question in biology. The relevant events happened 4 billion years ago, the relevant chemistry is buried under 4 billion years of subsequent change. How do we judge progress on a problem where we may never directly witness the answer, only constrain it from multiple angles?

moments.title: Hooke sees 'cells'
moments.body: Hooke's 'Micrographia' shows the honeycomb structure of cork seen through his microscope. He calls them 'cells' after monastic rooms.
moments.takeaway: The word 'cell' is born — applied to dead plant walls.

moments.title: Schleiden and Schwann
moments.body: Schleiden states all plants are made of cells; Schwann extends it to animals. Cells become the universal unit of life.
moments.takeaway: All life is cellular.

moments.title: Virchow's 'omnis cellula e cellula'
moments.body: Virchow declares every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. Spontaneous generation is finally rejected for cellular life.

quote.text: Omnis cellula e cellula.

moments.takeaway: Cells reproduce. The cell theory is complete.

moments.title: Single-cell biology
moments.body: Single-cell RNA-sequencing identifies thousands of distinct cell types in the human body. The Human Cell Atlas project aims to catalogue them all.
moments.takeaway: Cell theory now operates at single-cell resolution.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Single-cell omics and live-cell imaging now reveal cellular diversity in unprecedented detail. The Human Cell Atlas is mapping all human cell types.
now.open_questions: How many distinct cell types exist in the human body?

items.reflection: Hooke saw dead walls and named them 'cells'. The name stuck though it was misleading. How does early terminology shape later science?

moments.title: Anthrax
moments.body: A small-town country doctor isolates Bacillus anthracis from infected sheep and grows it in pure culture. He demonstrates the bacterium causes anthrax — the first proof of bacterial disease.
moments.takeaway: A country doctor proves a bacterium causes disease.

moments.title: Tuberculosis bacillus
moments.body: Koch identifies the tubercle bacillus on 24 March 1882, the day still celebrated as World TB Day. TB kills 1 in 7 people in Europe at the time. He wins the 1905 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The cause of the era's biggest killer is identified.

moments.title: Koch's postulates
moments.body: Koch lays out four postulates for establishing causation: organism present in disease, isolated in pure culture, causes disease in animals, re-isolated. Modern epidemiology's foundation.
moments.takeaway: A logical framework for identifying pathogens.

moments.title: Modified postulates
moments.body: Koch's postulates have been modified for viruses, asymptomatic carriers, microbiomes. Molecular Koch's postulates (Falkow, 1988) extend them to virulence genes.
moments.takeaway: Koch's framework is updated but still active.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: TB still kills ~1.5 million people/year. The full bacterial pangenome is sequenced. Multi-drug-resistant TB and HIV-coinfection remain major challenges.
now.open_questions: Can we develop better TB vaccines and shorter treatments?

items.reflection: Koch demonstrated that a microscopic organism caused a major killer. Why is germ theory still resisted in some communities?

moments.title: Wallace's Ternate letter
moments.body: Wallace, ill with malaria in the Indonesian archipelago, has an insight: species evolve by natural selection. He writes it up and sends it to Darwin — the only Englishman he thinks will understand.
moments.takeaway: A naturalist in malaria-stricken Indonesia derives natural selection independently.

moments.title: Joint Linnean reading
moments.body:
Lyell and Hooker arrange a joint reading at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Wallace's letter and Darwin's earlier draft are presented together. Neither author is present.

The meeting goes unnoticed. The president declares the year produced 'no striking discoveries'.
moments.takeaway: The most consequential biological idea of the century is read to silence.

moments.title: Origin of Species
moments.body: Spurred by Wallace's letter, Darwin rushes 'On the Origin of Species' to press. The first run sells out in a day.
moments.takeaway: A rival's letter pushes Darwin to publish 20 years of careful work.

moments.title: Wallace's legacy
moments.body: Wallace becomes a leading biogeographer (Wallace's Line divides Asian and Australian fauna). He generously cedes priority to Darwin. He campaigns against vaccination, for spiritualism, and for land reform.
moments.takeaway: Wallace is gracious in defeat — and remains a credible co-discoverer.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Wallace's Line is studied by every biogeographer. The combined Darwin-Wallace framework underlies all of modern evolutionary biology.
now.open_questions: How important were independent discovery races in the development of evolutionary thinking?

items.reflection: Wallace generously credited Darwin. How often does scientific gentleness shape who gets credit?

moments.title: Mendel rediscovered
moments.who: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak
moments.body: Three botanists, working independently, rediscover Mendel's 1866 paper. Genetics is finally taken seriously, 34 years after Mendel published.
moments.takeaway: Mendel's neglected paper is rediscovered three times in one year.

moments.title: Hardy-Weinberg
moments.body: A British mathematician and a German doctor independently derive the Hardy-Weinberg principle: allele frequencies remain stable in large random-mating populations.
moments.takeaway: Population genetics gains its null hypothesis.

moments.title: Fisher, Haldane, Wright
moments.who: R. A. Fisher, J. B. S. Haldane, Sewall Wright
moments.body: Three theoretical biologists derive the mathematics of population genetics, showing that Mendelian inheritance is fully compatible with Darwinian gradualism.
moments.takeaway: Mendel meets Darwin via mathematics.

moments.title: Modern synthesis books
moments.body: Dobzhansky's 'Genetics and the Origin of Species' (1937), Huxley's 'Evolution: The Modern Synthesis' (1942), Mayr's 'Systematics' (1942), and Simpson's 'Tempo and Mode' (1944) crystallise the modern synthesis.
moments.takeaway: Evolution becomes a unified, mathematical theory.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The 'extended evolutionary synthesis' adds epigenetics, developmental bias, niche construction. Genome-wide association studies probe the genetic basis of adaptation.
now.open_questions: How much can selection alone explain? What role does drift, mutation bias and epigenetics play?

items.reflection: Mendel's paper was ignored for 34 years. How do we ensure today's important papers don't suffer the same fate?

moments.title: Chromosomes carry genes
moments.body: Sutton (a Kansas graduate student) and Boveri (Würzburg) independently propose that Mendel's hereditary units sit on chromosomes — the Sutton-Boveri theory.
moments.takeaway: Genes have a physical location.

moments.title: Morgan's white-eyed fly
moments.body: Morgan, initially sceptical of Mendelism, finds a single white-eyed male fly in his 'fly room' at Columbia. Tracking the mutation through generations, he proves chromosomes carry genes. 1933 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A single mutant fly converts a sceptic into the founder of modern genetics.

moments.title: First genetic map
moments.body: At 19, undergraduate Sturtevant maps fruit-fly genes by recombination frequencies. The first genetic map of a chromosome.
moments.takeaway: An undergraduate invents genetic mapping in one night.

moments.title: X-ray mutagenesis
moments.body: Muller (Morgan's student) shows X-rays cause mutations. The link between radiation and genetic damage is established. 1946 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Mutations can be induced — and counted.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Drosophila remains a key model organism. The fly genome was sequenced in 2000. Single-fly genomics, optogenetics and CRISPR have made Drosophila even more powerful.
now.open_questions: Can fly biology continue to inform human disease, ageing, neuroscience?

items.reflection: Morgan started out a Mendel sceptic. How often do scientists who switch sides become the new field's founders?

moments.title: Griffith's transformation
moments.body: Griffith finds that heat-killed virulent pneumococcus can 'transform' live non-virulent strains into killers. Some 'transforming principle' transfers the trait. He doesn't know what it is.
moments.takeaway: Heredity can be transferred between bacteria.

moments.title: Avery, MacLeod, McCarty
moments.who: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty, Rockefeller
moments.body: After 10 years of work, they identify the transforming principle as DNA — not protein, as most expected. Avery is 67 and a year from retirement. He never receives a Nobel.
moments.takeaway: DNA is the genetic material. Recognition is slow.

moments.title: Hershey-Chase confirms
moments.who: Alfred Hershey, Martha Chase, Cold Spring Harbor
moments.body: Using radio-labelled phage proteins and DNA, Hershey and Chase show that only DNA enters bacteria — protein doesn't. Avery is finally vindicated.
moments.takeaway: Definitive proof DNA carries heredity.

moments.title: Double helix
moments.body: Within months of Hershey-Chase, the double helix structure is published. DNA goes from 'transforming principle' to molecular icon in nine years.
moments.takeaway: From mystery to icon in less than a decade.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: DNA is the basis of all genetics, biotechnology, forensics, ancestry. The cost of sequencing a human genome has fallen by ~10^6 since 2001.
now.open_questions: What other macromolecules can encode heritable information? RNA, prions, methylation marks?

items.reflection: Avery's 1944 paper changed biology, but he wasn't given a Nobel. Why does it sometimes take society decades to recognise foundational discoveries?

moments.title: Priestley restores air
moments.body: Priestley puts a mouse in a sealed jar — it dies. He adds a sprig of mint — and the mouse can live. Plants 'restore' air. He doesn't know that what plants produce is oxygen.
moments.takeaway: Plants change the air. We now know they produce oxygen.

moments.title: Ingenhousz adds sunlight
moments.body: Ingenhousz, the empress's physician, shows plants only restore air in sunlight — and not at night. He doesn't see leaves; he sees photosynthesis.
moments.takeaway: Sunlight powers the air-restoration.

moments.title: Calvin's tracer cycle
moments.who: Melvin Calvin, James Bassham, Andrew Benson, Berkeley
moments.body: Calvin uses radioactive 14C and paper chromatography to trace the carbon path through photosynthesis. The Calvin (or Calvin-Benson-Bassham) cycle is mapped step by step. Calvin alone wins the 1961 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Photosynthesis is decoded molecule by molecule.

moments.title: Mitchell's chemiosmosis
moments.body: Working in a privately-funded estate lab in Cornwall, Mitchell proposes ATP is made by a proton gradient across membranes. He is ridiculed for years. 1978 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A privately funded eccentric solves bioenergetics.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Photosynthesis converts ~100 GtC/yr of CO2 into biomass. Synthetic biology aims to improve the efficiency of Rubisco. Artificial photosynthesis for green H2 is a major research target.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer C3 crops with C4 photosynthesis? Can we make artificial photosynthesis competitive with solar PV?

items.reflection: Mitchell ran his lab on a private estate after being marginalised by academia. How does science treat its eccentrics?

moments.title: Helmholtz on muscle
moments.body: Helmholtz measures muscle contraction times and energy use, founding muscle physiology. He shows it follows thermodynamic laws — no 'vital force'.
moments.takeaway: Muscle is a thermodynamic engine.

moments.title: Sliding filament theory
moments.who: H. E. Huxley & J. Hanson; A. F. Huxley & R. Niedergerke
moments.body: Two papers, in the same issue of Nature, propose the sliding-filament theory. Two filaments — thin actin and thick myosin — slide past each other during contraction.
moments.takeaway: Muscle contracts by molecular sliding, not coiling.

moments.title: Huxley's swinging cross-bridge
moments.body: Andrew Huxley proposes the cross-bridge cycle: myosin heads attach to actin, pivot, detach, reattach further along. ATP powers each cycle.
moments.takeaway: A motor protein walking along an actin track.

moments.title: Single-molecule motors
moments.body: Optical traps observe single myosin molecules taking steps along actin. The motor walks ~5 nm per ATP. Cytoskeletal motors (kinesin, dynein, myosin) are now studied at single-molecule scale.
moments.takeaway: Biology's molecular motors can be watched, atom by atom.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Muscle disease therapies target the cross-bridge cycle (e.g. mavacamten for HCM). Cytoskeletal motors are tracked in living cells. Optogenetic control of motors is being developed.
now.open_questions: Can synthetic biology engineer molecular motors with novel cargo?

items.reflection: Two competing groups published sliding-filament theory back-to-back in 1954. How does scientific competition shape discovery?

moments.title: Squid giant axon
moments.body: Cole and Curtis show the squid giant axon — large enough to push a microelectrode into — is an ideal system for studying nerve impulses. WWII interrupts.
moments.takeaway: A 1 mm-diameter squid axon enables modern neurophysiology.

moments.title: Hodgkin-Huxley equations
moments.body: Hodgkin and Huxley publish four papers in J. Physiology, modelling the action potential as time-varying Na+ and K+ conductances. The equations remain the foundation of computational neuroscience. 1963 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A 70-year-old mathematical model still works.

moments.title: Patch clamp
moments.body: Neher and Sakmann develop the patch clamp — recording from single ion channels. They prove channels are discrete molecular gates. 1991 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Single ion channels can now be observed individually.

moments.title: K+ channel structure
moments.body: MacKinnon solves the structure of the K+ channel by X-ray crystallography. The 'selectivity filter' explains how K+ passes but Na+ doesn't. 2003 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The structural basis of nerve signalling is revealed.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Connectomics, optogenetics, BCIs and brain organoids extend electrophysiology. Channelopathies (epilepsy, arrhythmia) are now genetically diagnosed and targetable.
now.open_questions: Can we record from every neuron in a small brain in real time? How does action-potential coding produce thought?

items.reflection: Hodgkin and Huxley's 1952 equations are still taught. Few biology papers age so well. What makes their model so robust?

moments.title: Pancreas and diabetes
moments.body: Minkowski and von Mering accidentally remove a dog's pancreas; the dog develops diabetes. The pancreas must produce something controlling sugar.
moments.takeaway: The pancreas regulates blood sugar.

moments.title: Banting and Best
moments.who: Frederick Banting, Charles Best, J. J. R. Macleod, Toronto
moments.body: Banting, a surgeon, persuades Macleod to let him try to isolate the pancreatic hormone. Best, a medical student, is his assistant. In months they extract insulin from dog pancreas and save a diabetic dog.
moments.takeaway: Two amateurs in Toronto cure a 'death sentence' disease.

moments.title: Leonard Thompson
moments.body: Leonard Thompson, 14, weighing 65 lb and dying from diabetes, becomes the first patient treated with insulin. He lives another 13 years.
moments.takeaway: A teenager becomes the first diabetic saved by insulin.

moments.title: Nobel controversy
moments.body: Banting and Macleod share the 1923 Nobel. Banting, furious that Best was omitted, splits his prize with him; Macleod splits his with biochemist James Collip. The patent is sold for $1 — Banting refusing to profit from a life-saving drug.
moments.takeaway: Insulin is given to the world for $1.

moments.title: Insulin pricing crisis
moments.body: In 2024, a vial of insulin can cost $300 in the US — despite Banting's wish. Generic insulin, modern analogs, and patent disputes have made insulin affordability a major political issue.
moments.takeaway: Banting sold the patent for $1; modern insulin is among the most expensive drugs.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Insulin is now produced by recombinant DNA in E. coli (Genentech, 1978). Closed-loop 'artificial pancreas' systems combine continuous glucose monitors with insulin pumps. ~500 million people have diabetes globally.
now.open_questions: Can stem-cell-derived beta cells cure type 1 diabetes? Can GLP-1 analogues (Ozempic, etc.) reshape diabetes care?

items.reflection: Banting refused to profit from insulin. A century later, US insulin can be unaffordable. What duty do scientists have to their inventions?

moments.title: Lindeman's trophic dynamics
moments.body: Lindeman, 26, publishes 'The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology' just months before dying of liver disease. He shows energy flows through ecosystems in discrete trophic levels, with ~10% efficiency at each step.
moments.takeaway: Ecology becomes quantitative. The author dies before its impact is recognised.

moments.title: Odum's ecosystem ecology
moments.body: The Odum brothers develop ecosystem-level energy budgets. Their textbook 'Fundamentals of Ecology' (1953) defines the field for a generation.
moments.takeaway: Ecology becomes a discipline with textbooks and methods.

moments.title: Silent Spring
moments.body: Carson's book exposes DDT's effects on bird populations. Bald eagles and peregrine falcons nearly extinct in the US recover after DDT is banned in 1972. The book launches the modern environmental movement.
moments.takeaway: Pesticides bioaccumulate up food chains, with catastrophic effects.

moments.title: Trophic downgrading
moments.body: Modern ecology studies how loss of apex predators cascades down food webs (wolves in Yellowstone, sharks in oceans). Trophic cascades are central to conservation.
moments.takeaway: Lindeman's framework now guides global conservation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: DNA metabarcoding lets ecologists identify entire food webs from environmental DNA. Camera traps and acoustic monitoring extend ecological observation. Earth-system models incorporate biosphere-atmosphere coupling.
now.open_questions: Can rewilding restore ecosystem function in human-dominated landscapes?

items.reflection: Lindeman died at 27 with one paper. It still defines ecology. Can one paper change a field?

moments.title: Gaia at JPL
moments.body: NASA hires Lovelock to design life-detection instruments for Mars. Looking at Earth's atmosphere — far from chemical equilibrium — he realises life maintains it. Mars's atmosphere is dead and at equilibrium; Earth's is alive.
moments.takeaway: Earth's atmosphere is itself a sign of life.

moments.title: Gaia hypothesis published
moments.body: Lovelock and microbiologist Lynn Margulis publish the Gaia hypothesis: Earth's biosphere actively regulates climate and chemistry to suit life. The hypothesis is attacked as teleological.
moments.takeaway: Life and planet co-evolve, the authors argue. Critics call it mysticism.

moments.title: Daisyworld
moments.body: Daisyworld — a toy model with black and white daisies — shows how life could regulate planetary temperature without consciousness or design. The model defuses the teleology charge.
moments.takeaway: Self-regulation can emerge mechanically from selection.

moments.title: Earth-system science
moments.body: Modern Earth-system science draws heavily on Gaia. IPCC models couple biology, geochemistry and climate. Gaia is now mainstream — under a different name.
moments.takeaway: Gaia has been absorbed into mainstream Earth-system science.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Planetary boundaries (Rockström et al.) define safe operating limits for humanity. Earth-system models track multiple coupled cycles. Climate change is, in Lovelock's late framing, Gaia's response to civilisation.
now.open_questions: Can the biosphere recover from anthropogenic perturbations? What planetary boundaries are most fragile?

items.reflection: Lovelock proposed Gaia as a metaphor; it became a science. When are metaphors useful, when misleading?

moments.title: Gurdon's frog
moments.body: Gurdon transplants nuclei from intestinal cells into enucleated frog eggs and grows adult frogs. Differentiation is reversible. He shares the 2012 Nobel with Yamanaka.
moments.takeaway: Differentiated nuclei retain all genetic information — and can be reprogrammed.

moments.title: ES cells
moments.body: Mouse embryonic stem cells (1981) and human ES cells (1998) revolutionise developmental biology. But human ES use is ethically contested.
moments.takeaway: Pluripotent cells can be cultured indefinitely — but human ES cells require destroying embryos.

moments.title: Yamanaka factors
moments.body: Yamanaka and his student Takahashi screen 24 candidate genes and find that just four (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) can reprogram adult fibroblasts to pluripotent stem cells. 2012 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Adult cells can be reset to embryonic state with four genes.

moments.title: iPS in the clinic
moments.body: iPS-derived retinal pigment epithelial cells, dopaminergic neurons and CAR-T cells enter clinical trials. iPS cells are now standard in disease modelling and drug screening.
moments.takeaway: Reprogrammed cells become medicine.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: iPS cells are used worldwide. CRISPR-edited iPS cells model genetic disease. Direct reprogramming bypasses pluripotency entirely.
now.open_questions: Can iPS-derived organoids replace organ transplants? Can we reverse cellular ageing safely?

items.reflection: Yamanaka's discovery removed the ethical objection to ES cells overnight. How often does technology dissolve ethical impasses?

moments.title: Van Leeuwenhoek's animalcules
moments.body: Van Leeuwenhoek examines his own dental plaque under a homemade microscope and sees 'a little white matter... animalcules a-moving very prettily'. He has discovered the human microbiome.
moments.takeaway: The microbiome is observed 350 years before it is named.

moments.title: Escherich finds E. coli
moments.body: Pediatrician Escherich isolates E. coli from infant faeces. The bacterium becomes one of the most-studied organisms in biology.
moments.takeaway: The model organism of microbiology is found in babies.

moments.title: Human Microbiome Project
moments.body: Metagenomic sequencing reveals 100 trillion microbes in the average human — outnumbering our cells. Skin, gut, mouth, vagina have distinct ecosystems. Differences correlate with obesity, IBD, depression.
moments.takeaway: We are walking ecosystems of microbes.

moments.title: Faecal microbiota transplant
moments.body: A clinical trial in Amsterdam shows FMT cures recurrent C. difficile infection more effectively than antibiotics. FMTs become a recognised therapy.
moments.takeaway: Transferring entire microbial communities cures disease.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Microbiome research links gut bacteria to obesity, autoimmune disease, cancer immunotherapy response, neurodegenerative disease. Therapeutic 'next-gen probiotics' are in clinical trials.
now.open_questions: How specific are microbiome-disease links? Can we engineer microbiomes therapeutically?

items.reflection: Van Leeuwenhoek saw the microbiome in 1676. We are still understanding what it does. Why is the closest biology so hard to study?

moments.title: Ehrlich's side chains
moments.body: Ehrlich proposes antibodies are 'side chains' on cells that bind specific antigens. He develops Salvarsan, the first effective drug for syphilis. 1908 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Antibodies are envisioned as specific molecular recognition.

moments.title: Clonal selection
moments.body: Burnet proposes the clonal selection theory: each lymphocyte makes one antibody; antigens select clones to multiply. The framework is confirmed in the 1960s.
moments.takeaway: The immune system is a Darwinian process inside the body.

moments.title: Köhler and Milstein make monoclonals
moments.body: Köhler and Milstein fuse antibody-producing B cells with immortal myeloma cells, creating hybridomas that make unlimited identical antibody. They share the 1984 Nobel; they decline to patent it.
moments.takeaway: Monoclonal antibodies — invented, given to the world.

moments.title: Antibody drugs
moments.body: Monoclonal antibodies are now the leading class of drugs — Humira, Keytruda, Rituximab, Trastuzumab. Bispecifics and antibody-drug conjugates expand the toolbox.
moments.takeaway: Antibodies are now top-selling drugs.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Antibody therapies dominate oncology, autoimmune disease, infectious disease (COVID). Bispecific antibodies, CAR-T cells, antibody-drug conjugates extend the platform.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer antibodies that cross the blood-brain barrier? Can phage display fully replace immunisation?

items.reflection: Köhler and Milstein didn't patent monoclonal antibodies. The technology is now a >$200B/year industry. How do we balance generosity with the sustainability of basic research funding?

moments.title: Restriction enzymes
moments.body: Arber, Nathans and Smith discover restriction enzymes — molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific sequences. 1978 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: DNA can be cut precisely. Engineering becomes possible.

moments.title: Cohen and Boyer's hybrid
moments.body: Cohen and Boyer insert a frog gene into a plasmid and put it back into E. coli. The first recombinant organism. They (and Stanford) patent the technique.
moments.takeaway: Genes can be moved between species. Biotech is born.

moments.title: Genentech
moments.body: Genentech is founded — the first biotech company. In 1978 it produces recombinant insulin in E. coli; in 1982 it is the first biotech drug approved.
moments.takeaway: Academic recombinant DNA becomes industrial biotech.

moments.title: Asilomar Conference
moments.body: At Asilomar, leading molecular biologists pause recombinant DNA research and self-impose safety guidelines. It is a rare example of effective scientific self-regulation.
moments.takeaway: Scientists agree to police themselves on potential biohazards.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Recombinant DNA underpins biotech, pharma, agriculture and synthetic biology. mRNA vaccines (COVID), CAR-T cell therapies, and gene therapies all rely on it.
now.open_questions: Can we ethically engineer human germline cells? Can synthetic biology design organisms safely?

items.reflection: Asilomar showed scientists could self-regulate. Why has this not been replicated for AI or CRISPR?

moments.title: Jacob-Monod operon model
moments.who: François Jacob, Jacques Monod, Pasteur Institute
moments.body: Jacob and Monod propose the lac operon: a regulator gene encodes a repressor that controls transcription. The concept of gene regulation is born. 1965 Nobel (with Lwoff).
moments.takeaway: Genes are regulated, not just inherited.

moments.title: Monod's 'Chance and Necessity'
moments.body: Monod's bestselling book argues random chemistry + selection makes biology. Becomes a touchstone of late-20th-century scientific atheism.
moments.takeaway: Molecular biology meets philosophy.

moments.title: Transcription factors
moments.body: Hundreds of transcription factors are identified in eukaryotes. Regulation becomes a vast combinatorial system.
moments.takeaway: Gene regulation in animals is vastly more complex than in bacteria.

moments.title: Regulatory genomics
moments.body: Genome-wide assays map enhancers, promoters, methylation marks. The 'regulatory code' is being decoded — slowly. Many disease-associated SNPs are in regulatory regions.
moments.takeaway: Most variation in disease is regulatory, not coding.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Gene regulation is central to development, disease, and synthetic biology. CRISPR-based gene activation/inhibition lets us probe regulatory networks rapidly.
now.open_questions: Can we predict gene expression from sequence alone? What is the regulatory code?

items.reflection: Monod said 'man knows at last that he is alone in the universe's unfeeling immensity'. How does molecular biology shape worldview?

moments.title: Mereschkowsky and Wallin
moments.body: Russian botanist Mereschkowsky (1905) and American Wallin (1920s) propose chloroplasts and mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. They are ignored or ridiculed.
moments.takeaway: Endosymbiosis is proposed twice — and twice forgotten.

moments.title: Margulis rediscovers
moments.body: Margulis's paper 'On the Origin of Mitosing Cells' is rejected by 15 journals before publication. She argues eukaryotes formed by endosymbiotic mergers of prokaryotes.
moments.takeaway: Endosymbiosis is rediscovered — and dismissed by 15 journals.

moments.title: Molecular vindication
moments.body: Mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes are sequenced and shown to be most closely related to free-living α-proteobacteria and cyanobacteria respectively. Margulis is vindicated.
moments.takeaway: Sequencing proves a once-derided hypothesis.

moments.title: Lateral gene transfer everywhere
moments.body: Endosymbiosis is now one of several known mechanisms of major evolutionary innovation. Lateral gene transfer is widespread among prokaryotes; mitochondrial transfer is found in some animal lineages too.
moments.takeaway: Major transitions in evolution come from cellular mergers.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Eukaryotic cells are evolutionary chimeras. The 'archaea + bacterium' merger that produced LECA is now estimated at ~2 billion years ago. Recent work points at Asgard archaea as our archaeal ancestor.
now.open_questions: Was there one symbiosis event or several? How did the nucleus arise?

items.reflection: Margulis's paper was rejected by 15 journals. She was right. What does that say about peer review?

moments.title: PE proposed
moments.body: Eldredge and Gould observe that fossil species often appear suddenly and remain stable for millions of years before disappearing — punctuated equilibrium. Speciation is rapid and rare; stasis is the norm.
moments.takeaway: Evolution may be rapid bursts in small populations, not slow grades.

moments.title: Adaptationism wars
moments.body: Gould and Lewontin's 'Spandrels' paper (1979) attacks reductionist adaptationism. Dawkins, Maynard Smith and others defend gene-centred evolution. The debate splits the field.
moments.takeaway: Evolution gets its loudest in-house controversy of the late 20th century.

moments.title: Both/and
moments.body: Modern syntheses incorporate gradualism and punctuation, gene-centred and developmental views. Eldredge and Gould's challenge has been absorbed.
moments.takeaway: PE is now part of mainstream evolutionary theory.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Genome-wide adaptive events, hybridisation-driven speciation and rapid bursts in cichlid fish illustrate PE-style dynamics. Evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo) reframes Gould's concerns.
now.open_questions: How rapid is the fastest speciation? What roles do regulatory genes play?

items.reflection: Gould was a brilliant essayist; many of his arguments have been moderated. How does writing skill shape scientific influence?

moments.title: Hamilton's inclusive fitness
moments.body: Hamilton's rule (rb > c) explains altruism: a behaviour spreads if it benefits relatives weighted by relatedness. Hamilton derives it as a graduate student; he is largely ignored.
moments.takeaway: Altruism becomes mathematically explicable.

moments.title: E.O. Wilson's 'Sociobiology'
moments.body: Wilson's massive synthesis applies evolutionary thinking to animal — and, in the last chapter, human — social behaviour. Some Harvard colleagues, including Gould and Lewontin, accuse him of biological determinism.
moments.takeaway: Evolutionary thinking extends to human behaviour — controversially.

moments.title: Dawkins's 'Selfish Gene'
moments.body: Dawkins popularises Hamilton's gene-centred view in 'The Selfish Gene'. The book becomes the most-read book in evolutionary biology of the century.
moments.takeaway: The gene's-eye view captures public imagination.

moments.title: Behavioural ecology
moments.body: Modern behavioural ecology rigorously tests evolutionary explanations of behaviour using field experiments, comparative methods, game theory and genomics.
moments.takeaway: Animal behaviour is now firmly evolutionary.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Sociobiology is largely accepted for animals. Human behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology and cultural evolution coexist uneasily. Genome-wide studies illuminate social traits.
now.open_questions: How much of human behaviour has genetic basis? How does cultural evolution interact with biological?

items.reflection: Wilson was attacked physically (pitchers of water) at scientific meetings in the 1970s. Why are evolutionary applications to humans so contentious?

moments.title: Mitchell's chemiosmosis
moments.body: Working in a private estate, Mitchell proposes that ATP is synthesised by a proton gradient across membranes. The idea is ridiculed for a decade. 1978 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Energy currency comes from proton gradients, not direct chemistry.

moments.title: Boyer's binding change
moments.body: Boyer proposes ATP synthase has three catalytic sites that cycle through binding, catalysis and release. His mechanism is mechanical.
moments.takeaway: A rotating molecular machine, predicted from biochemistry.

moments.title: Walker's structure
moments.body: Walker's X-ray structure of F1 ATP synthase shows asymmetric subunits — confirming Boyer's binding change. Boyer and Walker share the 1997 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The structure proves the rotating mechanism.

moments.title: Rotation observed
moments.body: A Japanese team attaches an actin filament to ATP synthase's central stalk and watches it rotate directly under the microscope. The molecular motor is seen in action.
moments.takeaway: A single ATP synthase molecule is seen to rotate — one of biology's most beautiful experiments.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: ATP synthase runs in every cell of every organism. It produces our body weight in ATP per day. Drugs targeting bacterial ATP synthase (bedaquiline) treat MDR-TB.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer ATP synthase variants? Can synthetic mimics power devices?

items.reflection: Boyer predicted rotation from biochemistry alone. Twenty years later it was seen directly. How often does theory precede observation in molecular biology?

moments.title: Rous's chicken virus
moments.body: Rous shows a virus can cause chicken sarcoma. The result is dismissed for decades — cancer is supposed to be non-infectious. He wins the 1966 Nobel at age 87.
moments.takeaway: Some cancers are caused by viruses. The discoverer waits 55 years for recognition.

moments.title: Cellular src
moments.body: Varmus and Bishop find that Rous's viral oncogene src has a normal cellular homolog. Cancer comes from corrupted normal genes, not foreign DNA. 1989 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Cancer genes come from within.

moments.title: p53 tumour suppressor
moments.body: p53 is discovered as a tumour-associated antigen; in 1989 it is recognised as a tumour suppressor mutated in >50% of human cancers.
moments.takeaway: Tumour suppressors are the brakes; oncogenes are the accelerators.

moments.title: Imatinib
moments.body: Imatinib (Gleevec) targets the BCR-ABL fusion protein in CML. Five-year survival jumps from 30% to 95%. The first targeted cancer drug.
moments.takeaway: Understanding oncogenes leads to molecular cancer therapy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cancer genomes are routinely sequenced. Targeted therapies, CAR-T, checkpoint inhibitors and ADCs have transformed many cancers. mRNA cancer vaccines are in trials.
now.open_questions: Can we cure metastatic solid tumours? Why do immunotherapies work for some patients but not others?

items.reflection: Rous's chicken virus result was dismissed for decades. How does establishment scepticism slow medical progress?

moments.title: PD-1 discovered
moments.body: Honjo's lab identifies PD-1, an immune checkpoint receptor that prevents T cells from attacking. He doesn't yet know its therapeutic potential.
moments.takeaway: An immune brake is identified.

moments.title: Allison blocks CTLA-4
moments.body: Allison shows that blocking CTLA-4 (another checkpoint) unleashes T cells to kill cancer. Pharmaceutical companies are sceptical for years.
moments.takeaway: Releasing immune brakes can cure cancer.

moments.title: Ipilimumab approved
moments.body: Ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) becomes the first checkpoint inhibitor approved, for metastatic melanoma. Some patients live a decade or more.
moments.takeaway: Metastatic melanoma, once almost universally fatal, now has long-term survivors.

moments.title: Allison and Honjo Nobel
moments.body: The 2018 medicine Nobel honours their work. Anti-PD-1 drugs (Keytruda, Opdivo) are now used in dozens of cancers.
moments.takeaway: Checkpoint inhibitors are now standard cancer therapy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are approved for ~20 cancer types. Combinations with other agents extend the benefit. Some patients show durable cures.
now.open_questions: Why do only some patients respond? Can we predict and improve response?

items.reflection: Allison persuaded pharma companies for years. How often is the path from discovery to clinic blocked by commercial scepticism?

moments.title: Bateson's homeotic mutations
moments.body: Bateson coins 'homeosis' for mutations where one body part is transformed into another (e.g. an antenna becoming a leg in flies). He doesn't know the cause.
moments.takeaway: Mutations can rewire body plans.

moments.title: Lewis on bithorax
moments.body: Lewis genetically dissects the bithorax complex in Drosophila — a series of genes controlling segment identity. 1995 Nobel (with Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus).
moments.takeaway: A cluster of genes maps to body segments in linear order.

moments.title: Homeobox discovered
moments.who: Matthew Scott, William McGinnis, Ernst Hafen
moments.body: A conserved 180-bp DNA sequence — the homeobox — is found in many homeotic genes. Stunningly, the same Hox genes appear in flies, mice and humans, in the same linear order along the chromosome.
moments.takeaway: All animals share a deeply conserved set of body-plan genes.

moments.title: Eye gene
moments.body: Gehring's group shows the mouse Pax6 gene, expressed ectopically in a fly leg, induces a fly eye. Master regulators of organ formation are conserved across 600 million years.
moments.takeaway: A mammalian eye gene can build a fly eye.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Evo-devo has shown body plans arise from small changes in regulatory networks. The Hox genes are still studied for cancer, regeneration, evolution.
now.open_questions: How did the Hox cluster evolve from a single ancestral gene?

items.reflection: Mice and flies share the same body-plan genes. We diverged 600 million years ago. What does this tell us about the unity of life?

moments.title: Hayflick limit
moments.body: Hayflick shows normal human cells divide ~50 times in culture, then stop. The 'Hayflick limit' was thought to be experimental error — cells should be immortal.
moments.takeaway: Normal cells have a finite division count.

moments.title: Tetrahymena telomeres
moments.body: Blackburn sequences the ends of Tetrahymena chromosomes and finds tandem repeats — telomeres. The structure protects chromosome ends.
moments.takeaway: Chromosome ends have special protective sequences.

moments.title: Telomerase
moments.body: Blackburn and her PhD student Greider discover telomerase, the enzyme that maintains telomeres. They share the 2009 Nobel with Szostak.
moments.takeaway: An enzyme replenishes chromosome ends — but only in some cells.

moments.title: Telomeres and disease
moments.body: Short telomeres are associated with ageing, dyskeratosis congenita, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Most cancers reactivate telomerase to become immortal.
moments.takeaway: Telomeres link ageing to cancer.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Telomere length is a biomarker of ageing. Telomerase inhibitors are being trialled in cancer. Telomerase activators are controversial 'anti-ageing' supplements.
now.open_questions: Can telomere maintenance therapies extend healthspan safely?

items.reflection: The Hayflick limit was initially considered an artefact. How long does it take for a 'limit' to become a deep principle?

moments.title: Kerr observes apoptosis
moments.body: Pathologist Kerr observes cells dying in a tidy, regulated way — shrinking, fragmenting — distinct from necrosis. He calls it 'shrinkage necrosis', later renamed 'apoptosis' (Greek: leaves falling).
moments.takeaway: Some cell deaths are programmed, not accidental.

moments.title: C. elegans cell death genes
moments.body: Horvitz, working in Sydney Brenner's C. elegans, identifies the cell-death genes ced-3, ced-4, ced-9. Each one of the worm's 1090 cells has a defined fate. Brenner, Sulston and Horvitz share the 2002 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Genes that kill cells are conserved across animals.

moments.title: Caspases and Bcl-2
moments.who: Vishva Dixit, John Reed and others
moments.body: The mammalian caspases (homologs of ced-3) and Bcl-2 family (homologs of ced-9) are identified. Cancer cells over-express Bcl-2 to avoid apoptosis.
moments.takeaway: Cancer is partly a failure of apoptosis.

moments.title: BH3-mimetic drugs
moments.body: Venetoclax — a BH3 mimetic that triggers apoptosis — is approved for CLL. Death genes become drug targets.
moments.takeaway: Programmed death is now a drug target.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Apoptosis underlies development, immunity, cancer therapy. Other regulated cell death modes (necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis) are now recognised.
now.open_questions: Can controlling cell death cure neurodegeneration? Heart attack injury?

items.reflection: Cell death turns out to be precisely controlled. How does a fundamentally negative process become a positive force in biology?

moments.title: De Mairan's mimosa
moments.body: Astronomer de Mairan shows mimosa leaves open and close on a ~24-hour cycle even in constant darkness. Plants have internal clocks.
moments.takeaway: Living things keep time internally.

moments.title: period gene in flies
moments.body: Benzer's lab identifies fly mutants with abnormal sleep cycles. The Period gene is the first known clock gene.
moments.takeaway: A single gene tunes daily rhythm.

moments.title: Cloning PER
moments.who: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, Michael Young
moments.body: Three groups in the US clone PER and dissect the negative-feedback loop that produces 24-hour oscillations. They share the 2017 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Daily rhythms come from a molecular feedback loop.

moments.title: Chrono-medicine
moments.body: Drug effects vary with time of day (chronopharmacology). Shift work is now classified as a probable carcinogen. Light therapy treats seasonal affective disorder.
moments.takeaway: Time of day matters for medicine.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Clock genes are conserved from cyanobacteria to humans. Every tissue has its own clock, synchronised by the SCN in the brain. Chrono-medicine is a growing field.
now.open_questions: Can chronotherapy improve cancer outcomes? Can we mitigate shift-work harm?

items.reflection: De Mairan's 1729 mimosa experiment was right. It took 250 years to find the gene. How long can we live with a phenomenon before mechanism?

moments.title: Patient H.M.
moments.who: William Scoville, surgeon; Brenda Milner, neuropsychologist
moments.body: Surgeon Scoville removes H.M.'s hippocampi to treat seizures. H.M. survives but cannot form new long-term memories. Milner's studies show the hippocampus is essential for declarative memory.
moments.takeaway: A single surgical accident reveals the brain's memory system.

moments.title: LTP discovered
moments.body: At Oslo, Bliss and Lømo show high-frequency stimulation of hippocampal neurons strengthens synapses for hours — long-term potentiation. The plausible cellular basis of memory.
moments.takeaway: Memory at the synapse level.

moments.title: NMDA receptor
moments.body: LTP requires the NMDA glutamate receptor — a voltage- and ligand-gated channel that serves as a coincidence detector. Memory has a molecular substrate.
moments.takeaway: A specific receptor is necessary for learning.

moments.title: Kandel Nobel
moments.body: Kandel's decades of work on Aplysia and mouse memory wins the 2000 Nobel. He shows short- and long-term memory involve distinct molecular pathways.
moments.takeaway: Memory has a molecular logic.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Memory engrams can be optogenetically labelled and reactivated in mice. Drugs and electrical stimulation are being tested for memory enhancement. Alzheimer's disease research targets synaptic loss.
now.open_questions: Where exactly is a specific memory stored? Can we restore lost memories?

items.reflection: H.M. died not knowing his case had revolutionised neuroscience. He had no memory of consenting to the studies. What consent ethics apply when patients can't remember?

moments.title: Hales weighs plants
moments.body: Clergyman-scientist Hales measures water uptake by sunflowers and shows leaves lose much water by transpiration. He coins the cohesion-tension idea for how water rises in plants.
moments.takeaway: Plants are pumped by sunlight evaporating water from leaves.

moments.title: Stomata seen
moments.body: Microscopists identify stomatal pores in leaves. Guard cells regulate opening based on water status.
moments.takeaway: Plants have controllable pores for gas exchange.

moments.title: Cohesion-tension theory
moments.body: Dixon and Joly explain how water can be sucked up 100-m trees: water's cohesion (hydrogen bonds) allows it to be pulled under tension. The xylem is under negative pressure.
moments.takeaway: Trees pull water up via a column under metastable tension.

moments.title: Drought and climate
moments.body: Cavitation (xylem embolism under drought) is killing forests worldwide. Stomatal behaviour determines how plants respond to elevated CO2.
moments.takeaway: Plant water relations now matter for global climate.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Plants transpire ~40% of land precipitation back to the atmosphere. Drought-tolerant crop varieties are a major breeding target. Mass tree death from drought is increasing.
now.open_questions: Can crops be engineered to use water more efficiently? Will rising CO2 mitigate or exacerbate plant water stress?

items.reflection: Hales saw water rising in plants in 1727. The full mechanism took 200 years. Why are plant physiology mechanisms so hard?

moments.title: First AIDS cases
moments.body: CDC reports five cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia in previously healthy gay men. A new immune disease — AIDS — is emerging. Within years it is a global pandemic.
moments.takeaway: A modern pandemic begins with five case reports.

moments.title: HIV identified
moments.who: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier; Robert Gallo
moments.body: Pasteur Institute scientists isolate the AIDS virus (LAV); Gallo's group at NIH names it HTLV-III. Years of priority dispute follow. Barré-Sinoussi and Montagnier share the 2008 Nobel; Gallo does not.
moments.takeaway: AIDS has a viral cause. Credit is bitterly contested.

moments.title: AZT, first antiretroviral
moments.body: AZT (zidovudine) is the first effective HIV drug — though briefly, since the virus rapidly mutates resistance. The era of antiretroviral therapy begins.
moments.takeaway: HIV is treatable. Briefly.

moments.title: HAART
moments.body: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (three drug combination) suppresses HIV durably. People with HIV begin to live near-normal lifespans. From death sentence to chronic disease in 15 years.
moments.takeaway: HAART transforms HIV from fatal to manageable.

moments.title: Cure cases and PrEP
moments.body: Stem-cell transplants cure two patients (Berlin, London) — a proof of principle for HIV cure. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) prevents transmission. Long-acting injectables further reduce risk.
moments.takeaway: HIV is preventable and, in rare cases, curable.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: ~39 million people live with HIV. ~75% are on ART. Mortality has dropped 70% since the peak. Vaccine attempts have repeatedly failed; broadly neutralising antibodies offer new hope.
now.open_questions: Can we cure HIV more broadly than transplants? Can we develop an effective vaccine?

items.reflection: AIDS denialism in South Africa under Mbeki caused an estimated 330,000+ deaths. How can science communication better counter pseudo-science?

moments.title: C. elegans connectome
moments.body: After decades of reconstruction from electron micrographs, Brenner's group publishes the wiring diagram of the entire C. elegans nervous system — 302 neurons, ~7,000 connections.
moments.takeaway: The first complete connectome — a 302-neuron worm.

moments.title: Human Connectome Project
moments.body: Multi-institutional project maps human white-matter pathways with diffusion MRI. The macroscopic human connectome is published.
moments.takeaway: The human brain's wiring is mapped at the millimetre scale.

moments.title: Fly brain hemisphere
moments.body: Electron microscopy reconstructs ~25,000 neurons and ~20 million synapses in half the fruit-fly brain.
moments.takeaway: A whole insect brain mapped at synapse resolution.

moments.title: Cubic millimetre of human cortex
moments.body: A 1 mm^3 piece of human cerebral cortex is reconstructed at synaptic resolution: ~57,000 cells, 150 million synapses, 1.4 petabytes of data.
moments.takeaway: Slowly, the human brain is being reconstructed neuron by neuron.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Connectomics increasingly uses ML for image reconstruction. Goal: full mouse brain connectome (~70 million neurons). Eventually, the human cortex.
now.open_questions: How much does the connectome reveal about function? Will it explain consciousness?

items.reflection: C. elegans took decades for 302 neurons. Human brain has 86 billion. When does scale outrun any feasible approach?

moments.title: First gene therapy trial
moments.body: Anderson treats two girls with ADA-SCID by retroviral transfer of the ADA gene. Limited success.
moments.takeaway: The first attempt at human gene therapy.

moments.title: Jesse Gelsinger dies
moments.body: Jesse Gelsinger, 18, dies of immune reaction during a gene therapy trial. The death pauses the field for years and tightens oversight.
moments.takeaway: A tragic death halts a field.

moments.title: AAV success stories
moments.body: Adeno-associated virus vectors deliver functional genes safely. Glybera (LPL deficiency, 2012), Luxturna (RPE65 retinitis, 2017), Zolgensma (SMA, 2019) are approved. Some cost >$2 million per dose.
moments.takeaway: Single-gene diseases become curable — at extreme cost.

moments.title: Casgevy approved
moments.body: Casgevy, a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle cell disease, is approved in the UK and US.
moments.takeaway: CRISPR therapy enters the clinic.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: ~30 gene therapies are approved. Trials are underway for muscular dystrophy, haemophilia, retinal disease, neurological diseases. Prime editing and base editing extend the toolkit.
now.open_questions: Can gene therapy be made cheap enough for the world's poor? Can in vivo CRISPR be made safer?

items.reflection: Gelsinger's death pushed the field back by years. How should risk be balanced against potential cure in untested therapies?

moments.title: Fleming and penicillin
moments.body: Fleming notices mould kills bacteria on a contaminated plate. He nearly throws the plate away. Florey, Chain and Heatley turn it into a usable drug a decade later.
moments.takeaway: The accidental discovery that launches modern medicine.

moments.title: First resistance
moments.body: Even before penicillin is widely deployed, an enzyme (penicillinase) is identified that breaks down penicillin. Resistance is intrinsic to bacterial populations.
moments.takeaway: Resistance precedes wide drug use — it just gets selected by it.

moments.title: MRSA
moments.body: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is identified within a year of methicillin's introduction. MRSA spreads globally; hospital-acquired infections rise.
moments.takeaway: Bacteria evolve resistance to new drugs in months.

moments.title: Plasmid-borne colistin resistance
moments.body: mcr-1, a plasmid-borne colistin resistance gene, is found globally within months of identification. Colistin is the last-resort antibiotic against MDR Gram-negatives.
moments.takeaway: Resistance now spreads via mobile genetic elements at planetary scale.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: AMR is projected to cause 10 million deaths/year by 2050. The antibiotic pipeline is thin. Phage therapy, bacteriocins and microbiome modulation are being explored.
now.open_questions: Can we develop antibiotics faster than bacteria evolve resistance?
