items.reflection: Fleming warned about overuse of penicillin in his 1945 Nobel lecture. The warning was ignored. Why do we so often ignore foundational warnings?

moments.title: Mendel and peas
moments.body: Mendel chooses peas — easy to grow, easy to cross, with seven discrete traits — and discovers the laws of heredity. The right model organism makes the right insight possible.
moments.takeaway: Choosing the right organism shapes what you can discover.

moments.title: Morgan's flies
moments.body: Morgan's fly room at Columbia establishes Drosophila as the genetic workhorse. Cheap, fast, mappable.
moments.takeaway: Drosophila becomes the genetic model.

moments.title: Brenner picks C. elegans
moments.body: Brenner proposes a tiny nematode (~1 mm, 959 cells, transparent) as the model for developmental biology and neuroscience. He, Sulston and Horvitz share the 2002 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A worm becomes the most extensively studied animal in biology.

moments.title: Mouse ES cells
moments.who: Martin Evans, Matt Kaufman, Gail Martin
moments.body: Mouse ES cells enable genetic engineering of mammals. Knockout mice transform medical research. Evans wins the 2007 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Mice become bespoke disease models.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Models include zebrafish, frogs, yeast, E. coli, Arabidopsis, Tetrahymena, naked mole-rats, octopuses, planaria. iPSC-derived organoids extend modelling to human cells.
now.open_questions: Can organoids replace some animal experiments? Can in silico models replace others?

items.reflection: Brenner picked a worm because it was tractable. Mendel picked peas. How much does choice of organism shape discovery?

moments.title: Karikó's mRNA work
moments.body: Karikó spends decades trying to make mRNA into a drug. She is demoted, denied funding, refused tenure. Her work on modified nucleosides finally solves the immune-response problem in 2005.
moments.takeaway: A scientist persists through years of rejection.

moments.title: Modified nucleotides
moments.body: Karikó and Weissman show pseudouridine-substituted mRNA escapes innate immune detection. The modification makes mRNA therapeutically viable.
moments.takeaway: A simple modification transforms a class of drug.

moments.title: Lipid nanoparticles
moments.body: BioNTech and Moderna develop LNP delivery for mRNA. Initial focus is on cancer vaccines. The technology is ready when COVID hits.
moments.takeaway: A solution waits for a problem.

moments.title: COVID vaccines
moments.body: mRNA vaccines for SARS-CoV-2 are designed in days and tested in months. Within 11 months of the genome being released, vaccines are approved. Billions of doses are given.
moments.takeaway: From genome to vaccine in 11 months — a record.

moments.title: Karikó-Weissman Nobel
moments.body: The 2023 medicine Nobel honours their persistence. Karikó's daughter was a US Olympic rower; she once joked she had two gold medals at home (and didn't yet have a Nobel).
moments.takeaway: Decades of perseverance, finally recognised.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: mRNA vaccines are in trials for cancer, HIV, influenza, RSV. The platform is fast, flexible, programmable. Concerns about durability and rare side effects remain.
now.open_questions: Can mRNA therapeutics treat genetic disease in vivo?

items.reflection: Karikó was demoted multiple times. Her work saved millions of lives. How do institutions miss extraordinary persistence?

moments.title: cAMP discovered
moments.body: Sutherland finds cyclic AMP as a 'second messenger' between hormones and intracellular responses. 1971 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Hormones don't act directly — they act via internal messengers.

moments.title: G proteins
moments.body: Gilman and Rodbell identify G proteins that couple receptors to internal signalling. They share the 1994 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A class of switches between receptors and second messengers.

moments.title: GPCR structures
moments.body: Lefkowitz and Kobilka solve the first GPCR structures, including the β2-adrenergic receptor captured in active state. 2012 Nobel. About 30-40% of approved drugs target GPCRs.
moments.takeaway: The molecular details of signal transduction are visualised.

moments.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists
moments.body: Semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) — GLP-1 receptor agonists — are reshaping diabetes and obesity therapy worldwide.
moments.takeaway: A single class of receptor drugs reshapes obesity treatment.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: GPCRs are the largest druggable target class. Structural biology, cryo-EM and ML are advancing GPCR drug design rapidly.
now.open_questions: Can biased agonists separate desired from undesired effects? Can allosteric drugs offer better selectivity?

items.reflection: 30-40% of drugs target GPCRs. Why is one class of receptor so disproportionately tractable for drugs?

moments.title: Stevens and Wilson
moments.who: Nettie Stevens, Bryn Mawr; E. B. Wilson, Columbia
moments.body: Independently and almost simultaneously, Stevens (studying mealworms) and Wilson identify a sex-determining chromosome. Stevens clearly states the XY model first; Wilson is more cautious. Stevens dies of breast cancer in 1912 at 50.
moments.takeaway: Sex is determined chromosomally. Stevens publishes first; the credit goes to Wilson.

moments.title: Barr body
moments.body: Barr identifies a stained body in female nuclei — the inactivated X chromosome. Mary Lyon (1961) shows random X inactivation.
moments.takeaway: One X is silenced. Females are mosaics for X-linked genes.

moments.title: XXY syndrome
moments.body: Jacobs identifies XXY chromosomes in Klinefelter syndrome and X0 in Turner syndrome. Chromosomal sex disorders join cytogenetics.
moments.takeaway: Chromosomal variation explains many sex-related disorders.

moments.title: SRY gene
moments.body: SRY, the male-determining gene on the Y chromosome, is identified. It encodes a transcription factor that switches gonad development toward male.
moments.takeaway: A single gene tips the developmental balance.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Y chromosome has lost most of its genes over evolutionary time. Atypical sex chromosomes are increasingly identified in genomic data.
now.open_questions: Will the Y chromosome continue to degenerate? How does intersex variation relate to gender identity?

items.reflection: Nettie Stevens published the XY model first but was overshadowed by Wilson. How often do historic female scientists vanish from textbooks?

moments.title: Spemann and Mangold
moments.body:
Mangold (Spemann's PhD student) transplants a small region of one amphibian embryo into another and grows a second embryo with two body axes. The 'organiser' induces surrounding tissue.

Mangold dies in a kitchen explosion at 26 before her thesis is published. Spemann wins the 1935 Nobel alone.
moments.takeaway: Cells can instruct neighbours to form whole organs. A student dies before her Nobel-worthy thesis is recognised.

moments.title: Molecular identity of the organiser
moments.body: Genes such as Goosecoid, Chordin, Noggin are identified as molecular components of the organiser. The signal molecules antagonise BMP, inducing neural tissue.
moments.takeaway: The organiser's signals are molecularly identified.

moments.title: Patterning gradients
moments.body: Morphogen gradients (Wnt, BMP, FGF, Shh) pattern embryos. Concentration thresholds determine cell fate.
moments.takeaway: Embryos are patterned by gradient chemistry.

moments.title: Synthetic embryology
moments.body: Synthetic mouse and human embryo-like structures are grown from stem cells. The blastoid era raises new ethics questions.
moments.takeaway: Embryos can be assembled from cells in a dish.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Single-cell omics map developmental decisions. CRISPR screens identify required genes. Synthetic embryology challenges definitions of human embryo.
now.open_questions: Where is the ethical line for synthetic embryo research?

items.reflection: Mangold died in a kitchen accident at 26. Spemann's Nobel mentions her but she shares no credit. How do we honour young scientists whose lives were cut short?

moments.title: Hill reaction
moments.body: Hill shows isolated chloroplasts can produce oxygen and reduce non-natural electron acceptors. The light reactions are separable from carbon fixation.
moments.takeaway: Photosynthesis splits into light and dark reactions.

moments.title: Z-scheme
moments.body: Hill and Bendall propose the Z-scheme: two photosystems in series, with electrons pumped up the energy ladder by two photon absorptions. The scheme remains correct.
moments.takeaway: Two photons per electron, in series.

moments.title: PSII crystal structure
moments.body: The 1.9 Å structure of photosystem II reveals the water-oxidising Mn4CaO5 cluster — the most catalytic centre on Earth, splitting water at neutral pH and room temperature.
moments.takeaway: The most important catalytic cluster on Earth is finally seen at atomic resolution.

moments.title: Artificial photosynthesis
moments.body: Solar-fuel research aims to mimic the water-splitting half of PSII with metal-oxide catalysts. Some prototypes reach 10%+ solar-to-hydrogen efficiency.
moments.takeaway: Artificial leaves are being engineered, atom by atom.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Photosynthesis fixes ~120 GtC/year. Crop yield gains from photosynthesis engineering (Rubisco, NPQ relaxation) are showing up in field trials.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer C3 crops with C4 efficiency? Can artificial photosynthesis become competitive with PV+electrolysis?

items.reflection: PSII performs reaction industrial chemistry can't yet match. Why is biology so far ahead of materials science here?

moments.title: Mystery of scrapie
moments.body: Alper shows scrapie (a sheep disease) is resistant to radiation that destroys nucleic acids. The agent might be protein only. Few believe her.
moments.takeaway: A disease agent might be just protein — heretical to virology.

moments.title: Prusiner names prions
moments.body: Prusiner isolates the scrapie agent — a protein with no nucleic acid. He calls it a 'prion'. He is widely attacked. 1997 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A protein alone can be infectious.

moments.title: BSE-vCJD link
moments.body: BSE ('mad cow disease') is linked to a new variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. UK exports of beef are banned. Prion disease enters public consciousness.
moments.takeaway: Prion disease causes a public-health crisis.

moments.title: Misfolded proteins in neurodegeneration
moments.body: Amyloid-beta in Alzheimer's, alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, tau in many dementias propagate cell-to-cell prion-like. The 'prion paradigm' extends to common diseases.
moments.takeaway: Prion-like spreading may underlie major neurodegenerative diseases.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Prion diseases remain untreatable but rare. Lecanemab and donanemab (anti-amyloid antibodies) modestly slow Alzheimer's decline.
now.open_questions: Can prion-like spreading be blocked in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's?

items.reflection: Prusiner was attacked for proposing protein-only inheritance of disease. Now the paradigm is mainstream. Why is virology so resistant to non-nucleic-acid heredity?

moments.title: Boll discovers rhodopsin
moments.body: Boll observes a pink colour in frog retinas that bleaches in light. He has discovered rhodopsin, the visual pigment.
moments.takeaway: Vision involves a chemical that bleaches in light.

moments.title: Wald and vitamin A
moments.body: Wald shows vision pigments use vitamin A (retinal) bound to opsin proteins. Light isomerises retinal from 11-cis to all-trans, triggering vision. 1967 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Vision is a one-photon photochemical isomerisation.

moments.title: Cone opsin genes cloned
moments.body: Nathans clones the genes for three human cone opsins (blue, green, red) and rhodopsin. Colour vision has molecular basis. Many forms of colour blindness are explained.
moments.takeaway: Colour vision has a molecular code.

moments.title: Optogenetics
moments.body: Channelrhodopsin (a microbial opsin) is expressed in mammalian neurons. Light becomes a tool for controlling specific neurons in living animals.
moments.takeaway: Microbial opsins let neuroscientists control brains with light.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Optogenetics is now standard in neuroscience. Gene therapy for retinitis pigmentosa (RPE65 mutations) restores partial vision. Bionic eyes are being trialled.
now.open_questions: Can optogenetics treat human disease (e.g. restore vision)?

items.reflection: Wald studied a chemical reaction; Boyden and Deisseroth turned it into a tool. How do molecular discoveries become technologies?

moments.title: Beijerinck isolates Rhizobium
moments.body: Dutch microbiologist Beijerinck isolates the rhizobia that live symbiotically in legume root nodules. He shows they fix atmospheric N2.
moments.takeaway: Legumes harbour N-fixing bacteria, explaining ancient crop rotation.

moments.title: Haber-Bosch industrial
moments.body: Synthetic ammonia from N2 and H2. Industrial N fixation now exceeds natural biological fixation. Half of human bodies' nitrogen came from Haber-Bosch.
moments.takeaway: Industry overtakes biology in nitrogen fixing.

moments.title: Anammox bacteria
moments.body: Anaerobic ammonium-oxidising bacteria (anammox) are discovered. They are now estimated to account for 30-50% of ocean N2 production. Industrial nitrogen removal uses them too.
moments.takeaway: A whole branch of the N cycle was missed for over a century.

moments.title: Nitrogen crisis
moments.body: Reactive N (NO3-, NH4+, NOx) levels exceed planetary boundaries. Algal blooms, dead zones, eutrophication. NPK runoff is a defining environmental problem.
moments.takeaway: Too much N is now a planetary boundary problem.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Engineering cereals to fix their own N is an active research frontier. The nitrogen cycle is now a major Earth-system focus.
now.open_questions: Can we engineer cereals to fix their own nitrogen?

items.reflection: For most of Earth history, biological N fixation was rate-limiting for life. Now humans dominate the cycle. What are the consequences?

moments.title: Alvarez asteroid hypothesis
moments.who: Luis Alvarez, Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro, Helen Michel, Berkeley
moments.body:
The Alvarezes find a thin iridium-rich layer in K-Pg boundary clays worldwide. Iridium is rare on Earth's crust but abundant in asteroids. They propose an asteroid impact ended the dinosaurs.

The hypothesis is widely ridiculed. It is now consensus.
moments.takeaway: A single layer of iridium kills the dinosaurs.

moments.title: Chicxulub crater identified
moments.body: A 180-km buried impact crater off the Yucatan, Mexico, is dated to exactly the K-Pg boundary. The Alvarez hypothesis is vindicated.
moments.takeaway: The smoking gun: a 10-km asteroid hit at the right time.

moments.title: Multi-stressor extinction
moments.body: More detailed studies show Deccan volcanism contributed to environmental stress; the asteroid was the coup de grâce.
moments.takeaway: Mass extinctions usually have multiple causes.

moments.title: Sixth extinction
moments.body: Modern extinction rates are 100-1000x background; biologists call it the Sixth Mass Extinction. The cause this time is human activity.
moments.takeaway: Humans are causing a mass extinction event in real time.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Five recognised mass extinctions in the fossil record. The Sixth is underway. Conservation prioritises hotspots, captive breeding, rewilding.
now.open_questions: How much biodiversity can we save? Can de-extinction work for charismatic species?

items.reflection: The Alvarez hypothesis was ridiculed for a decade. How often does palaeontology need physics to break through?

moments.title: Landsteiner's blood types
moments.body: Landsteiner finds that mixing blood from different people sometimes causes agglutination. He identifies three (later four — A, B, AB, O) blood groups. Transfusion becomes safe. 1930 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Why transfusions sometimes killed patients — solved.

moments.title: Rhesus factor
moments.body: Rh antigens explain haemolytic disease of the newborn. Anti-D prophylaxis (1969) prevents most cases.
moments.takeaway: A second blood-group system is identified.

moments.title: ABO genetics
moments.body: The ABO gene encodes a glycosyltransferase. A and B alleles differ by four amino acids; O has a frameshift. The molecular basis is solved.
moments.takeaway: A 90-year mystery solved by molecular biology.

moments.title: Universal blood
moments.body: Enzymatic conversion of A and B blood to O has been demonstrated. Manufactured red cells from iPS cells are being trialled.
moments.takeaway: Universal blood, at last, is on the horizon.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Blood transfusion is one of the safest medical procedures. >100 million units transfused annually. Pathogen-reduced blood, manufactured red cells advance the field.
now.open_questions: Can manufactured blood replace donors entirely?

items.reflection: Before Landsteiner, transfusion was a 50-50 lottery. How many small discoveries make modern medicine routinely safe?

moments.title: First fossil hominins
moments.body: Neanderthal (Germany, 1856), Cro-Magnon (France, 1868), Java Man (Dubois, 1891), Piltdown Man (a fraud, 1912), Taung Child (South Africa, 1924 — Australopithecus). Human ancestry is gradually pushed back.
moments.takeaway: Europe long preferred a European ancestor; Africa turned out to be home.

moments.title: East African hominins
moments.who: Mary Leakey, Richard Leakey, Donald Johanson
moments.body: Olduvai (Zinjanthropus, 1959), Koobi Fora (KNM-ER 1470, 1972), Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis, 1974). Hominin diversity in Africa from 4 million years ago is established.
moments.takeaway: East Africa is the cradle of humanity.

moments.title: Neanderthal genome
moments.body: Pääbo's team sequences the Neanderthal genome from 40,000-year-old bones. They find that non-African humans carry 1-4% Neanderthal DNA. 2022 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Modern humans interbred with Neanderthals.

moments.title: Denisovans, Homo naledi, more
moments.body: Denisovans (from a finger bone), Homo naledi (a small-brained late survivor), Homo floresiensis (the 'hobbit'). The hominin family tree continues to expand.
moments.takeaway: Multiple hominin species coexisted with our ancestors.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Ancient DNA, dental calculus, isotope geochemistry now drive paleoanthropology. Multiple hominins overlap geographically and genetically.
now.open_questions: Why did we — Homo sapiens — survive when other hominins died out? Were they outcompeted, absorbed, or unlucky?

items.reflection: Piltdown Man was a fraud that lasted 40 years. How does science police its biases?

moments.title: Waddington coins 'epigenetics'
moments.body: Waddington proposes an 'epigenetic landscape' of developmental valleys. The term means above-genetic. He had no idea what the molecular basis would be.
moments.takeaway: Development is canalised, not direct gene expression.

moments.title: DNA methylation hypothesis
moments.body: Cytosine methylation is proposed as an epigenetic mark. Methylated DNA is associated with gene silencing.
moments.takeaway: A chemical mark on DNA controls gene expression.

moments.title: Histone code
moments.who: David Allis, Michael Grunstein and others
moments.body: Histone tails carry post-translational modifications (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation) that affect chromatin. The 'histone code' provides another epigenetic layer.
moments.takeaway: Histones carry combinatorial regulatory marks.

moments.title: Epigenetic editing
moments.body: CRISPR-dCas9 fused to methyltransferases or demethylases lets researchers add or remove epigenetic marks at specific sites — epigenetic editing.
moments.takeaway: Epigenetic marks can now be edited like genetic ones.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Epigenetics underlies cancer, ageing, development, behaviour. DNA methylation clocks ('Horvath clock') predict biological age.
now.open_questions: Can transgenerational epigenetic inheritance occur in humans? Can epigenetic reprogramming reverse ageing safely?

items.reflection: Waddington coined 'epigenetics' before he could know what it would mean. How often do scientific terms outlive their original definitions?
